# Why is my mix muddy?

> Why mixes turn muddy, where the problem lives in the spectrum, how to clear it with high-passing and wide cuts, and the causes that are not EQ problems at all.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/why-is-my-mix-muddy/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries, who make BEEFY.

---

It sounded enormous at two in the morning. In the car the next day it sounds like the whole record is playing through a duvet, and turning it up only makes the duvet louder.

A mix is muddy when too much energy is stacked between roughly 150 and 500 Hz, where the low mids of almost every instrument overlap. Fix it by cutting rather than boosting: high-pass everything that is not bass or kick, find the two or three tracks contributing most in that range and take 2 to 4 dB out of each with a wide cut, and check in mono, where mud is easier to hear. Reverb and too many layered parts are the other two usual causes.

## The short version

- **Where**: 150–500 Hz, the low mids

- **First move**: high-pass everything that is not kick or bass

- **Second**: wide 2–4 dB cuts on the worst two or three tracks

- **Third**: fewer layers, not more EQ

- **Reverb**: high-pass the returns around 300 Hz

- **Check**: mono, quiet, and on a small speaker

- **Why it stacks**: four equal parts sum to 6.02 dB above any one of them

- **Spread the cuts**: 2 dB off four tracks beats 8 dB off one, by 1 dB

- **Your room**: a 4.2 × 3.5 × 2.4 m room puts 20 axial modes in this range

**LIMIT** instead, everything else identical.

## Why that range and not another

Almost everything has energy between 150 and 500 Hz. The body of a kick, the fundamentals of a bass line, the warmth of a piano, the chest of a voice, the low end of a guitar, the room tone in a sampled break. Individually every one of them sounds right. Added together they produce a broad hump nobody chose, and because the ear reads that range as weight, the mix sounds heavy and unclear at the same time.

It compounds. Each track you add contributes a little more, so a mix gets muddier as it gets bigger, which is why the problem usually appears late in a session and feels like it came out of nowhere.

Measure the neighborhood before you argue with it. The span from 150 to 500 Hz is log2(500 / 150) = 1.74 octaves, out of the log2(20000 / 20) = 9.97 octaves between 20 Hz and 20 kHz. Take pink noise as a stand-in for a broadband record, equal energy in every octave, and that slice already holds 1.74 / 9.97 = 17.4% of the total, which is 7.6 dB below the whole-band level. Seventeen percent of the energy in a sixth of the spectrum, before a single part is stacked into it.

## How four polite tracks build a hump

Nobody puts the hump there deliberately. It assembles itself, and the arithmetic is the boring kind. Two uncorrelated sounds at the same level sum to 10 × log10(2) = 3.01 dB above either one. Four sum to 6.02 dB, six to 7.78 dB, eight to 9.03 dB. No single track is loud in the low mids. The sum is.

Quiet contributors still count, which is the part that hides the problem. A part sitting 3 dB under the main offender adds 10 × log10(1 + 10−0.3) = 1.76 dB to the pile. One 6 dB under adds 0.97 dB. One 10 dB under still adds 0.41 dB. Three of those together are worth more than a decibel, and not one of them looks like a problem when you solo it.

Now work out where a cut lands. Say four parts contribute equally at 250 Hz. Pull 8 dB out of the worst one and the sum falls by only 1.03 dB, because the other three never moved. Pull 2 dB out of all four and the sum falls by the full 2.0 dB. Half the depth on each, twice the result, and nothing sounds gutted. That is the entire case for wide, shallow and spread out over deep and surgical, and it is why a mix keeps sounding muddy after you have hollowed out one keyboard.

## One auditory filter at 250 Hz

Your ear does not read frequency off a fine ruler. It listens through a bank of overlapping filters, and two sounds landing inside one filter arrive as a single smeared event however clearly a spectrum display separates them. The accepted width for one of those filters, the equivalent rectangular bandwidth, is 24.7 × (4.37f / 1000 + 1) Hz. Run it across the mud range and the size of the problem shows up.

- **150 Hz**: 40.9 Hz wide, 130–170 Hz — about 4.8 semitones

- **200 Hz**: 46.3 Hz wide, 177–223 Hz — about 4.0 semitones

- **250 Hz**: 51.7 Hz wide, 224–276 Hz — about 3.6 semitones

- **300 Hz**: 57.1 Hz wide, 272–329 Hz — about 3.3 semitones

- **400 Hz**: 67.9 Hz wide, 366–434 Hz — about 2.9 semitones

- **500 Hz**: 78.7 Hz wide, 461–539 Hz — about 2.7 semitones

Read the right-hand column, because that is the one written in the language you compose in. At 250 Hz a single filter is 3.6 semitones wide, so the root and the minor third of a chord voiced down there land in the same slot and your ear gets one blurred event rather than two notes. At 150 Hz one filter is 4.8 semitones wide, close to a perfect fourth. The spectrum analyzer will show you two tidy peaks the whole time, which is why people trust their eyes and keep wondering what is wrong.

It also explains why the problem is a range rather than a frequency. The whole span from 150 to 500 Hz is 12 × log2(500 / 150) = 20.8 semitones, under two octaves, and it is covered by just over six auditory filters. Six slots for a kick body, a bass, a piano left hand, two guitars, a pad and a voice. There is no arrangement of a full band in which that does not get crowded.

## How to clear it

- High-pass every track that is not the kick or the bass, starting around 100 Hz and moving up until you hear the track thin out, then back off.

- Solo the mix bus in mono and listen for where it clouds.

- Sweep a narrow boost through 150 to 500 Hz on the biggest offender to find the exact frequency, then turn the boost into a wide cut of 2 to 4 dB.

- Do that on no more than three tracks. If you are cutting the same frequency on ten tracks, the arrangement is the problem.

- High-pass the reverb and delay returns around 300 Hz.

- Mute the least important layer entirely and see whether you miss it.

- Check again in mono, then on a phone.

## What a high-pass actually removes

Step one is the right first move, and it is worth knowing exactly how little of the mud range it touches. A high-pass is gentle above its corner. Here is a 12 dB per octave high-pass set to 100 Hz, measured across the band you are worried about.

- **50 Hz**: −12.30 dB

- **80 Hz**: −5.37 dB

- **100 Hz**: −3.01 dB, the corner

- **150 Hz**: −0.78 dB

- **200 Hz**: −0.26 dB

- **250 Hz**: −0.11 dB

- **300 Hz**: −0.05 dB

A tenth of a decibel at 250 Hz. Steepening the filter makes it worse, not better: at 24 dB per octave the same 100 Hz corner takes 0.17 dB at 150 Hz and nothing measurable at 250. To remove a usable 2 dB at 250 Hz with a 12 dB per octave high-pass you would have to put the corner at about 219 Hz, which also costs you 3 dB at 219 and everything below it. On a guitar that is a choice. On a piano it is vandalism.

So the high-pass and the wide cut do two different jobs and neither substitutes for the other. High-passing clears rumble, handling noise and sub content that no small speaker will ever reproduce, which frees up level and stops your limiter working on air. Clearing 150 to 500 Hz is the bell's job. If you have high-passed forty tracks and the mix is still cloudy, that is the expected outcome, not a sign that you did it wrong.

## Find the offender in one pass

Stop guessing and measure it. This takes about as long as reading the steps, and it replaces the hour normally spent nudging faders and hoping.

- Loop eight bars of the fullest section and leave it running.

- Collapse the master to mono.

- Mute one candidate track for four bars and note how much of the cloud leaves with it.

- Unmute, move to the next, and rank them. Anything whose removal changes nothing is innocent.

- On the top three only, put a bell at +6 dB with a Q around 1 and sweep 150 to 500 Hz.

- Flip the boost to a cut of 2 to 4 dB at the worst spot, then widen it until the cut stops sounding like a hole.

- Match the bypassed level to within a tenth of a dB before you decide anything.

Step three is the measurement and step five is only the aim. Keep each sweep under twenty seconds, because a +6 dB bell parked in one place retunes your ear and then it starts agreeing with you. If you have to mute five things before the mix opens up, no EQ move on any of them will do it and the honest answer is upstairs in the arrangement.

Level matching is where most cleanup gets fooled. Take 3 dB out of the low mids of three tracks and the whole mix gets quieter, and quieter loses every blind comparison it enters. The amplitude behind a decibel is 10−d/20: 1 dB is 0.891, 2 dB is 0.794, 3 dB is 0.708, 6 dB is 0.501. Put the difference back on the output before you judge whether the cut helped. [Gain staging](https://gazillionindustries.com/gain-staging/) covers the rest of it.

[BEEFY](https://gazillionindustries.com/beefy.html) will not fix mud — saturation adds harmonics into the range you are trying to clear. Clean first, then reach for weight.

**BEEF at 96.** Past where most settings want to live.

## The causes that are not EQ problems

**Too many parts.** Three instruments playing the same chord in the same octave is a mud generator no equalizer will defeat. Move one of them up an octave or take it out.

**Reverb on everything.** Reverb fills the gaps between notes, which is the definition of a less clear mix. Use fewer, shorter, and high-pass them.

**Mixing too loud, or in an untreated room.** Your ears hear more low end at high volume, so a mix balanced loud comes out light on bass and heavy in the low mids. A small room with no treatment exaggerates specific frequencies and hides others, which is why the car test exists.

**No high end.** Sometimes the mix is not muddy at all: it is dull. If nothing above 8 kHz is happening, the low mids sound proportionally larger. Check before cutting.

**Saturation applied before the low end was cleaned.** Harmonics arrive at whole-number multiples of what went in, so a rumbling 60 Hz component saturated on the way through produces 120, 180, 240, 300, 360, 420 and 480 Hz. Six of those seven harmonics land inside 150 to 500 Hz. High-pass the channel first and the same plugin makes half as much mess. [Harmonic distortion](https://gazillionindustries.com/harmonic-distortion/) has the mechanism.

**Stereo widening on low-mid material.** Width made by phase tricks rather than by panning survives on headphones and falls apart in a mono fold, so the pad you widened is one level on your monitors and another in a club, a phone, or a supermarket. [Phase cancellation](https://gazillionindustries.com/phase-cancellation/) and [mono compatibility](https://gazillionindustries.com/mono-compatibility/) cover what goes missing.

**The sample already had it.** A break lifted off a record arrives with its own room, its own bass and somebody else's low mids. Two of those stacked at the same tempo is four rooms. Cut on the sample rather than on everything you added around it.

## The room is doing some of it

Some of the mud is not in the file. Every rectangular room has axial modes at 343 / (2L) hertz and at every multiple of that, where 343 m/s is the speed of sound and L is the dimension in meters. A 4.2 by 3.5 by 2.4 meter bedroom puts its fundamentals at 40.8, 49.0 and 71.5 Hz, and their multiples climb straight into the range you are trying to judge.

Count them. Between 150 and 500 Hz that room has 20 axial modes, averaging 17 Hz apart, and two of them collide: 245.0 Hz is a multiple of both the 4.2 m and the 3.5 m dimension, and 285.8 Hz is a multiple of both the 4.2 m and the 2.4 m. At a coincidence like that the room does not politely add a decibel. You are mixing against peaks and nulls you did not put in the record.

The speaker placement has its own contribution. A monitor 0.6 m from the wall behind it sends a reflection back out of step at 343 / (4 × 0.6) = 143 Hz; pull it to 0.3 m and the cancellation moves up to 286 Hz, straight into the middle of the problem. Sit in a dip like that and you will hear too little at 286 Hz, add 3 dB to compensate, and ship a record that is 3 dB muddier than the one you thought you made.

The tell is simple. 250 Hz has a wavelength of 343 / 250 = 1.37 m, so a quarter wavelength is 34 cm. Move your head 34 cm and listen again. If the low mids change substantially, you were listening to the room. That is why the car works: it is a different wrong room, and two wrong rooms that agree are usually telling the truth.

## Muddy, boxy, boomy or just dark

Name it before you cut it, because four different complaints get called mud and three of them are somewhere else.

- **Boomy**: 60–120 Hz — one low note far louder than its neighbors, and it rings

- **Muddy**: 150–500 Hz — weight with no separation, words hard to follow

- **Boxy**: 300–600 Hz — the record sounds like it is in a cupboard

- **Honky**: 700 Hz–1.2 kHz — nasal, pinched, a megaphone quality

- **Dark**: nothing above 8 kHz — the low mids only sound bigger by comparison

The last one deserves a number, because cutting for it makes the record worse. On the pink stand-in above, 8 kHz to 20 kHz is 13.3% of the energy. Delete it entirely and the 150 to 500 Hz share rises from 17.4% to 20.1%, a shift of 0.62 dB. Two thirds of a decibel of extra low mid, and you did it by removing air rather than by adding weight. Restore the top end and the mud halves without an EQ node anywhere near 250 Hz.

## Where the cuts sit in the chain

Order changes the result more than any single setting. Corrective cuts go first on the channel, before the compressor. A 250 Hz build-up feeding a compressor makes the compressor pull the whole track down every time the build-up happens, so the part ducks on its own worst frequency and the mud survives with a pumping envelope attached to it.

High-pass before anything that adds harmonics. That is the arithmetic from the last section read in reverse: clean the fundamental you do not want, and the harmonics it would have generated in the mud range never exist. Saturating first and cutting after means removing the same energy twice, once as its cause and once as its effect.

Do the work on the channels and not on the master. A 2 dB cut at 250 Hz on the mix bus removes it from the kick body, the bass, the voice and the snare as well as from the three parts that caused it, and the record goes from cloudy to hollow in one move. The bus is for the last 0.5 dB after the channels are right.

Reach for a dynamic or multiband cut only when the build-up comes and goes. If 300 Hz is a problem when the pad plays and fine in the verse, a static bell is the wrong shape and a [multiband](https://gazillionindustries.com/multiband-compression/) or dynamic band that only moves when the energy arrives leaves the verse alone. Every other case, the static cut is simpler and sounds better.

## Doing it in your DAW

The arithmetic is identical everywhere and the stock tools all do this job. Three host details are worth knowing before you start.

In Ableton Live, EQ Eight has a per-band audition button that solos what the band is doing as you move it. Sweeping in audition finds the frequency faster than a +6 dB boost sweep and it does not retune your ear on the way, which matters because the boost sweep is the step in the list above with a twenty-second shelf life. Utility with Width at 0% is your mono check.

In Logic Pro, Channel EQ's low cut has selectable slopes, so you can put 12 and 24 dB per octave on the same corner and hear for yourself how little either one takes out of 250 Hz. The Gain plugin has a Mono switch on the output, which belongs on the master while you work.

In FL Studio the EQ lives on a mixer insert, so check which insert you are cutting: with tracks routed into submixes it is easy to take 3 dB out of a whole group while looking at one instrument's name. Fruity Parametric EQ 2 does the cuts, and the spectrum in Wave Candy will show you the hump you are aiming at.

- **Ableton Live**: EQ Eight for the cuts; Utility at 0% width for mono

- **Logic Pro**: Channel EQ with the low cut slope menu; Gain for mono

- **FL Studio**: Fruity Parametric EQ 2; Wave Candy for the spectrum

## Where it costs you

Over-correct and you get the opposite problem: a thin, brittle mix where every track has been high-passed into a narrow strip and the record has no weight at all. The low mids are where music lives, so the goal is to decide which instrument owns which part of that range, not to empty it. Aggressive high-passing on a sampled break also removes the room the break came with, which is usually the reason you chose it.

Put a bill on it. Cut 3 dB at 250 Hz on eight tracks and every one of them drops to 0.708 of its amplitude in the band that carried its body, while the sum in that band falls the full 3 dB. The record is clearer and it is also 3 dB lighter, and the usual reaction is to add 3 dB of saturation or a louder master to get the weight back. Now you have spent an evening moving energy out of the low mids and an hour putting harmonics into them.

The other cost is time. Mud is the most over-diagnosed fault in home mixing, and a fair share of sessions spent hunting 250 Hz were sessions where the arrangement had four parts in one octave, or the monitor was 30 cm off a wall. Check the room and the parts count first. They are free, and they are the two fixes that do not make the record smaller.

## What each failure sounds like

Faults have signatures. Learn the sound and you stop hunting, because the symptom names the cause.

- **Heavy, no separation, louder does not help**: the 150–500 Hz pile-up itself

- **Clear in solo, cloudy together**: masking — the fix belongs on the other tracks

- **One low note booms, the rest vanish**: a room mode or a resonant part, not a broad hump

- **Thin and brittle after an hour of cleaning**: over-high-passed; the body went with the rumble

- **Cloudy only when the pad enters**: arrangement, or a case for a dynamic band

- **Fine on monitors, muddy on headphones**: the room was hiding it, or width made by phase

- **Fine on headphones, muddy in the car**: a mono fold summing your centered low mids

- **Clean but small after cutting**: the cuts spent level and nothing put it back

- **Muddy and dull at the same time**: missing top end — add air before you cut weight

- **Gets muddier the louder you monitor**: your ears, not the mix — see [Fletcher–Munson](https://gazillionindustries.com/fletcher-munson/)

## Questions people ask

### How do you fix a muddy mix?

High-pass everything that does not need low end, make wide 2 to 4 dB cuts between 150 and 500 Hz on the two or three worst offenders, high-pass the reverb returns, and remove a layer. Check in mono throughout.

### What does a muddy mix sound like?

Heavy, unclear and indistinct, with no separation between instruments and lyrics that are hard to follow. Turning it up makes it louder but no clearer, which is the tell.

### How do you clean up muddy bass?

Decide which of the kick and the bass owns the bottom and which owns the body, then cut the other one there: commonly the kick keeps 60 to 90 Hz and the bass keeps 100 to 200 Hz. See [how to mix kick and 808](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-mix-kick-and-808/).

### What frequency causes muddiness?

Most often 200 to 400 Hz, with the surrounding range from about 150 to 500 Hz contributing. The exact frequency depends on the arrangement, so sweep and find it rather than cutting 250 Hz on everything out of habit.

### Should I cut 250 Hz on every track?

No, and the arithmetic says why. Cutting the same frequency everywhere lowers the whole record by that amount and changes no ratio between its parts, so the mix gets quieter and stays exactly as cloudy. Cut only the parts that failed the mute test, and leave the ones that need their body.

### How much should I cut at 300 Hz?

Two to four decibels, wide, on two or three tracks. Four parts each cut 2 dB take 2.0 dB off the pile; one part cut 8 dB takes off 1.03 dB and sounds hollow while doing it. If 4 dB is not enough, you have an arrangement problem rather than an EQ problem.

### Does high-passing everything fix a muddy mix?

Only partly, and less than people expect. A 12 dB per octave high-pass at 100 Hz removes 0.78 dB at 150 Hz and 0.11 dB at 250 Hz, so it clears rumble and sub content and leaves the mud range almost untouched. The wide cuts do that work.

### Why does my mix sound muddy on headphones but fine on my speakers?

Usually the room. Small rooms have peaks and nulls every few hertz through the low mids, and a null at 250 or 300 Hz hides a build-up you then never fix. Headphones have no room, so they show it. Move your head 34 cm and see whether the low mids change.

### Why does my mix sound muddy in the car?

A car sums a lot of content toward the middle and adds its own cabin resonances, so anything centered and stacked in the low mids gets emphasized twice. Check the mix in mono before you bounce; most of what a car exposes is already audible there.

### Is my room making my mix sound muddy?

Probably some of it. A 4.2 by 3.5 by 2.4 meter room has 20 axial modes between 150 and 500 Hz, roughly 17 Hz apart, with two frequencies where dimensions coincide. Test it by moving your listening position and by comparing on headphones and in a car. Two disagreeing rooms mean the room is talking.

### Does reverb make a mix muddy?

Yes, when the tail is longer than the gaps in the music. At 90 BPM a sixteenth note is 60000 / 90 / 4 = 166.7 ms, so a 2 second tail is still sounding 2000 / 166.7 = 12 sixteenths after the note that caused it. High-pass the return around 300 Hz and shorten the tail before you touch the dry tracks.

### Why does my mix get muddy as soon as I add the vocal?

The chest of a voice sits at roughly 150 to 300 Hz, on top of guitars, keys and the top of the bass. Cut the instruments rather than the voice, since the voice is the part people follow. See [how to EQ vocals](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-eq-vocals/).

### What is the difference between a muddy mix and a boxy mix?

Position. Mud is 150 to 500 Hz and reads as weight without separation. Boxiness is 300 to 600 Hz and reads as a small enclosed space around the sound. They overlap in the middle, which is why one cut sometimes fixes both complaints.

### Does saturation make a mix muddy?

It can, on material that still has low content. Harmonics land at whole-number multiples, so a 60 Hz component generates 120, 180, 240, 300, 360, 420 and 480 Hz, and six of those sit in the mud range. High-pass first and the same amount of saturation costs you far less. [Saturation explained](https://gazillionindustries.com/saturation-explained/) has the rest.

### Why is my mix muddy after mastering?

Limiting raises quiet material toward the peaks, and in most records the quiet material is low mid. A mix that was marginal at 250 Hz becomes plainly cloudy once 6 dB of gain reduction has compressed the distance between the hits and everything under them. Fix it in the mix, not at the master. See [how to master a beat](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-master-a-beat/).

### Should I use dynamic EQ or a static cut for mud?

Static when the build-up is always there, dynamic when it arrives with a particular part. A static bell that fixes the chorus takes the same energy out of a sparse verse that needed it, so match the tool to whether the problem has a schedule.

### How do I fix mud without losing warmth?

Assign the range rather than emptying it. Let one part own 150 to 250 Hz, another own 250 to 400, and cut each one where the other is living. Wide and shallow keeps the character; narrow and deep on everything is how a record ends up clear and cold.

## What BEEFY does

BEEFY is our saturation and loudness effect, and it is worth being clear about what it is for here. It adds body, squeezes space out of the peaks and brings out harmonics that help a sound feel bigger: useful on a thin kick or a polite break, and the opposite of what a cluttered low mid needs. **BEEF** adds weight and density, **COOK** moves the color from rounder toward brighter, and **JUICE** sets the input. Clear the range first, then decide what deserves the weight.

Order it the way the arithmetic above suggests. High-pass the channel, make the wide cut, and only then put BEEFY on the part that still needs weight, so the harmonics it generates are built from a fundamental you actually want. COOK moves the color from rounder toward brighter, and on a part that was already crowding the low mids the brighter end of it is the safer direction to take. **SOFT CLIP** and **LIMIT** are the two output switches, and the honest way to judge either of them is to match the bypassed level to a tenth of a dB first. BEEFY runs on Mac and Windows as AU, VST3 and standalone, and it is $19.

**SOFT CLIP** as the out stage, BEEF at 62. Match the bypassed level before you judge it.

Two in the morning is not a listening environment. The car, unfortunately, is.

# The Amen break

> Where the Amen break came from, why this break and not another, the 1986 compilation that pitched it down, and the fact that nobody in the band was ever paid.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/amen-break/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries, who make DRUGS.

---

A band in Atlanta needed something for the back of a single in the spring of 1969. They cut an instrumental over a gospel melody, the horns dropped out for four bars, and the drummer played alone. Nobody in that room got paid for what happened next.

The Amen break is a four-bar drum solo by Gregory C. Coleman, starting one minute and twenty-six seconds into The Winstons' "Amen, Brother", the B-side of their 1969 single "Color Him Father". It runs six or seven seconds depending on who is counting, and it became the rhythmic foundation of hip hop, jungle and drum and bass after it was reissued on a compilation in 1986. Neither the drummer nor the copyright holder ever received a royalty for any of it.

## The short version

- **Record**: The Winstons, "Amen, Brother", 1969, a B-side

- **Drummer**: Gregory C. Coleman, who died in 2006

- **Where**: 1:26 into the track, four bars, six or seven seconds

- **How it spread**: a 1986 breaks compilation, pitched down to 33 rpm

- **Royalties**: none, ever, to anyone in the band

- **Now**: added to the National Recording Registry in May 2026

**DOSE 12.** The line along the bottom is gain reduction.

## Why this break and not another one

There are thousands of drum breaks on soul records and only one of them ended up underneath three genres. The reasons are musical and they are worth knowing if you are looking for your own.

Coleman rides a ride cymbal rather than a hi-hat, which fills the space differently: a continuous wash instead of a tight pulse, so a producer can put anything on top without fighting for room. The snare has a distinctly pitched tone, so it reads as a note as well as a hit. The recording itself has a crunch to it, the sound of a small room and a hot signal path. And the four bars are not identical, so a loop of the whole thing has internal variation built in rather than repeating one bar four times.

Who actually devised it is contested. Richard Lewis Spencer, the bandleader who held the copyright, said he directed it. Phil Tolotta, the other surviving member, said the solo was "pure GC". That disagreement has never been settled and probably cannot be.

## What tempo the Amen break runs at

Sixteen beats, and the whole thing is over in about seven seconds. That gives you the tempo without looking anything up: sixteen beats divided by the length in seconds, times sixty. Or the same sum the short way, 960 divided by the seconds.

Seven seconds flat gives 960 ÷ 7.0 = 137.1 BPM. Seven and a twentieth gives 136.2. Six point nine gives 139.1, and 6.8 gives 141.2. A tenth of a second at the edge of your selection moves the answer by two BPM, which is the whole reason no two sources agree on a figure. They are not arguing about the record. They are arguing about where the four bars start and stop.

Measure your own copy rather than taking anybody’s number, including that one. Drop the file in, put the loop brace on the first hit of bar one and the first hit of the bar after, read the length in seconds, divide 960 by it. What comes back is the tempo of your transfer, and your transfer is the only one your session has to agree with.

Then accept that the figure is an average. Coleman is a man, not a clock, and the four bars drift inside themselves. If bar four runs 1% slow against an average of 137 BPM, that bar is 17.5 ms longer than the grid says: 1,750 ms stretched to 1,767. Seventeen milliseconds at the end of a phrase does not read as an error. It reads as a lean, it is most of why the loop breathes, and it is the first thing you destroy by warping every bar flat onto the grid.

## The detail almost nobody mentions

What early hip hop actually sampled was not the record. It was the 1986 *Ultimate Breaks and Beats* compilation, and that version was pitched down from 45 rpm to 33 and a third. So the Amen that entered the canon was slower and lower than the one The Winstons played, and every producer who built on it was building on a copy that had already been altered. The break most people know is a second-generation object.

## What 45 to 33 and a third actually did

Play a 45 at 33 and a third and you are running it at 33.333 ÷ 45 = 0.7407 of its speed. One number does everything, because on a turntable tempo, pitch and length are the same quantity wearing three names.

Tempo first: 137.1 × 0.7407 = 101.6 BPM. Pitch: 12 × log₂(0.7407) = −5.20 semitones, a perfect fourth down and then twenty cents further. Length: 1 ÷ 0.7407 = 1.35, so every decay in the recording got 35% longer. A cymbal that rang for 400 ms on the single rings for 540 ms on the compilation, and the room behind it swelled by the same 35%. The break did not only get lower and slower. It got bigger, because the early reflections of that small room stretched along with the drums inside it.

None of that is a story about a machine. It is what a speed change does, on a turntable in 1986 or in your session this afternoon, and it is why a break that has been slowed always sounds like a larger room than the one it was cut in. [Tape speed](https://gazillionindustries.com/tape-speed/) and [varispeed](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-varispeed/) run the same arithmetic on other material.

A speed change moving pitch, tempo and length together, so the paragraph above has something to point at. These are small moves on purpose: the slowed file is −1.30 semitones and the 1986 drop was −5.20, almost exactly four times further (5.20 ÷ 1.30 = 4.0). Hear a quarter of it and multiply.

- **Unity** — rate 1.0000, +0.00 semitones — https://gazillionindustries.com/skruu/skruu-dry.m4a

- **Slowed** — rate 0.9275, −7.25%, −1.30 semitones — https://gazillionindustries.com/skruu/skruu-down.m4a

- **Sped up** — rate 1.0779, +7.79%, +1.30 semitones — https://gazillionindustries.com/skruu/skruu-up.m4a

[DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html) is our free one-knob bus compressor for drums, voiced for exactly this kind of material: a break, a room, and everything squashed into one block.

## What producers did to it

In hip hop it was mostly looped and slowed. In jungle and drum and bass it was taken apart: sliced into individual hits, re-sequenced into patterns Coleman never played, time-stretched to tempos the recording was never near, and layered against itself. That second treatment is the reason the break outlived its own genre twice. A loop is a borrowing; a chopped break is an instrument.

If you want to work that way, [how to chop a drum break](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-chop-a-drum-break/) covers the method and [how to make drums sound dusty](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-drums-sound-dusty/) covers getting a modern recording into the same territory.

**DOSE 12.** The line along the bottom is gain reduction.

## How to squash the Amen break

Squashing the break means cutting its crest factor: pulling the loudest hits down, putting the same amount back, and letting the ride wash and the room come up underneath. The trade is better on this break than on most, because Coleman is on a ride and a ride never stops. Compress a tight hi-hat pattern and what rises is the gaps. Compress this and what rises is a continuous wash, which arrives as weight rather than as noise.

Two numbers tell you how far you went. Meter the loop and write down peak in dBFS and short-term loudness in LUFS, then subtract: a loop at −0.8 dBFS peak and −16.2 LUFS has a crest of 15.4 dB. Squash it, make the level back up, meter again, subtract again. The fall in that difference is the squash, in dB, and it is the only honest way to state it. [Crest factor](https://gazillionindustries.com/crest-factor/) has the long version.

Set the release off the grid rather than off a preset. At 137 BPM a sixteenth note is 60 ÷ 137 ÷ 4 = 109 ms. Compressor recovery is exponential, so one release time returns 63% of the gain (1 − 1/e) and three returns 95%. A 109 ms release is therefore two thirds back by the next sixteenth and all the way back three sixteenths later, at 328 ms. That surge repeats at 1 ÷ 0.109 s = 9.1 Hz, and 9 Hz is slow enough to follow and fast enough to hear as tremolo. Push the release out to a bar instead, 1,750 ms, and the loop sits down and stays down for the whole four. Both are usable. They are different records.

Attack is a frequency decision wearing a time label. Ten milliseconds is one full cycle of 100 Hz and ten cycles of 1 kHz, and the stick on that snare is mostly energy above 1 kHz, so a 10 ms attack lets the crack through and clamps the drum behind it. Drop to 0.1 ms, one cycle of 10 kHz, and the crack gets clamped with everything else. [What a transient is](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-a-transient/) covers the trade if it is new.

One more, and it is the one that gets missed. If the kick fundamental sits near 60 Hz, one cycle of it lasts 1,000 ÷ 60 = 16.7 ms. A detector with no high-pass on it follows that cycle, the gain ripples at 60 Hz, and the whole loop gets amplitude-modulated at 60 Hz. That puts a pair of sidebands 60 Hz either side of everything in the bar, and it turns up in the low mids as a grind no EQ will remove, because it is being manufactured downstream of the EQ.

### Do it

- Loop the four bars and set the session tempo to the figure you measured, not a round one.

- Meter the loop. Write down peak in dBFS and short-term loudness in LUFS, and subtract.

- Put one compressor on the drum bus with nothing else in the chain.

- High-pass the detector above the kick fundamental, 80 to 120 Hz.

- Set attack to 10 ms and release to one sixteenth note at your measured tempo.

- Push in until the meter reads 6 dB down on the loudest snare in the four bars.

- Add 6 dB of make-up gain.

- Meter again, subtract again, and write the new crest next to the old one.

- Bypass, match the two by loudness rather than by peak, and A/B them through a phone speaker.

Step nine is the one everybody skips and the only one that settles anything. Matched by peak instead of loudness, the squashed version is simply louder, and a louder version always wins. [How to compress drums](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-compress-drums/) works the same method on material that is not fifty-seven years old.

## Where the squash sits in the chain

Squash the whole break and then chop it, and every slice carries the same gain envelope, so the slices glue to each other when you replay them. Chop first and squash the rebuilt pattern, and the compressor is reacting to your pattern rather than to Coleman’s: a ghost note you dragged forward now pushes the ride around in a place it never did. Both work. They produce different instruments, and the second one is the jungle answer.

Order against pitch matters more than people expect, and the arithmetic is tidy. Compress at the original speed with a 109 ms release, render, then slow the render to 0.7407 and the release stretches with everything else to 109 ÷ 0.7407 = 148 ms. Slow first, then set a sixteenth at the new tempo of 101.6 BPM, and you get 60 ÷ 101.6 ÷ 4 = 148 ms. The same number, because slowing the tape slows the pump along with it. The order changes the sound only if you skip the sum.

Saturation before the compressor lifts the quiet parts first, so the compressor sees a flatter signal and grabs less than the meter led you to expect. Saturation after takes the block you have already built and rounds the tops off it. Filtering before is the detector high-pass by another route, since it changes what the sidechain sees whether you meant it to or not. [Drum bus chain order](https://gazillionindustries.com/drum-bus-chain-order/) walks the full list, and [parallel compression](https://gazillionindustries.com/parallel-compression/) is how you buy the density without spending the transients.

## What goes wrong, and what each one sounds like

Six failures, each with its own signature. Learn the sound and you stop guessing at the cause.

**Tremolo on the cymbals.** Release too short for the tempo. The wash swells and falls between hits at the sixteenth rate, around 9 Hz, and you start hearing the swelling instead of the drumming. Lengthen the release past one sixteenth.

**Crack with no drum under it.** Attack too long. The stick gets through untouched while the body behind it is clamped, and the snare arrives as a rim with the shell missing. Shorten the attack, or take less.

**Cardboard.** Attack too short. The stick is clamped along with everything else, every hit loses its front, and four bars of one of the great drum performances turn up sounding like hands on a phone book.

**The bars stop differing.** Too much of it. The four bars of the Amen are not identical, and that is half of why the loop survived fifty years of repetition. If bar three sat 2 dB above bar one and you have taken 8 dB off the peaks, those two bars now land within a decibel of each other, and a loop that used to move just repeats.

**The bleed arrives.** A squash lifts everything sitting under the hits: the room, the tape noise, the last of a horn chord that had not finished decaying when the drums took over. Some of that is the sound. All of it is permanent once you print it.

**Grind in the low mids.** The detector following the kick fundamental, described above. High-pass the detector and it goes.

Then the general cost, which is a bill rather than a fault. A squash trades dynamic range for density and it spends most of that range in places a phone speaker cannot send you, the room and the bottom of the kick. Something that opens up beautifully over monitors can reach a phone with nothing added at all. That is why step nine ends where it does.

## Getting it into your session at the right speed

Every DAW offers the same fork under a different name: one algorithm that moves time and holds pitch, and one that moves both together. The second is what the turntable did in 1986, and for a break you are slowing a long way it is usually the better sound and always the simpler sum.

In Ableton Live the fork lives in the clip’s Warp Mode chooser. Re-Pitch ties speed to pitch and does exactly the arithmetic above; Beats holds the pitch and repeats or skips material at the transients, which is convenient at small moves and audible as stutter at large ones. Logic Pro’s Flex Time gives you the same pair, one algorithm that cuts at transients and holds pitch and one that acts as a speed control. In FL Studio it is the sampler channel’s stretch setting, with a resampling option that behaves as a speed change. [Time stretching explained](https://gazillionindustries.com/time-stretching-explained/) covers what each family does to a transient on the way through.

Then the trap that actually bites, which has nothing to do with warping at all. If your break file is 44.1 kHz, your session runs at 48 kHz, and something in the path plays the samples out without converting them, the break runs at 48 ÷ 44.1 = 1.0884 times speed. That is 8.8% fast and 12 × log₂(1.0884) = 1.47 semitones sharp, so a break you measured at 137 BPM turns up at 149. If a loop will not sit on the grid and sounds a semitone and a half high, stop warping and go and look at the sample rates.

## The money

Nobody in The Winstons was ever paid for the sampling. Spencer held the copyright to the catalog and never licensed the break; the records that used it simply used it, in an era before sample clearance was routine and then in a genre that could not have afforded it. Coleman, by Spencer's account, died in poverty in February 2006.

Spencer's own verdict, to The Economist in 2011, is the line to quote: "[Coleman's] heart and soul went into that drum break. Now these guys copy and paste it and make millions." He described the whole thing as plagiarism and said he came from an era when you did not steal people's ideas.

In 2015 two British DJs ran a crowdfunding campaign to give him something. The goal was £1,000. It finished at £24,000 from 1,811 donations, and the cheque reached him in November of that year. His reaction, to the BBC: "They didn't have to do that — I didn't even know them. Fifty years on, some young white boys that I've never met, halfway across the world said, 'We're going to give you a gift.' It's probably one of the sweetest things that's happened to me in a long time."

He had already won a Grammy, for the A-side. "Color Him Father" took Best Rhythm & Blues Song at the ceremony in March 1970. He retired from music in 1971 and died in December 2020, aged 78. Who controls the copyright now is not stated anywhere public.

## How many records used it

No honest answer exists, only dated ones, because every figure in circulation traces back to a single user-submitted database with no published methodology. The BBC reported 1,862 in November 2015. NPR said at least 2,000 in 2017. Mixmag said over 2,500 in 2018. Those are the numbers with a source and a date attached; anything quoted as a current total is a number somebody read off a website that afternoon.

The other thing that shaped how people think about it is not a record at all. In 2004 the artist Nate Harrison made "Can I Get an Amen?", a seventeen-minute-and-forty-six-second lecture delivered over a locked groove of the break itself, arguing that the whole history of the loop is a history of copyright and of who gets to own a piece of culture. It has probably done more to teach producers about sampling law than any legal writing.

## Questions people ask

### What is the Amen break?

A four-bar drum solo played by Gregory C. Coleman on The Winstons' 1969 B-side "Amen, Brother", lasting six or seven seconds, which became the most reused piece of recorded drumming in popular music.

### Who played the Amen break?

Gregory C. Coleman, the Winstons' drummer. He died in February 2006, aged 61, and never received royalties from the sampling.

### Is the Amen break copyrighted?

Yes. It was never public domain. The copyright sat with the band's leader, Richard Lewis Spencer, who died in 2020; nothing public says who holds it now. The fact that it went uncollected for decades is not the same as it being free.

### Why is the Amen break used so much?

A ride cymbal instead of a hi-hat, a snare with a pitched tone, a crunchy room, and four bars that vary rather than repeat. Plus a 1986 compilation that put it in every producer's hands at once, already pitched down.

### What tempo is the Amen break?

Divide 960 by the length of the four bars in seconds. Seven seconds gives 137 BPM, 6.9 gives 139, 7.05 gives 136. Measure your own copy: a tenth of a second at the edge of the selection is worth two BPM, and the drummer drifts inside the bars anyway, so the answer is an average.

### How long is the Amen break?

Four bars, six or seven seconds depending on where you set the edges. Sixteen beats, always, and the beats are the safer thing to count.

### What key is the Amen break in?

It has no key. The snare has a pitched ring and the toms have fundamentals, but there is no harmony in four bars of drums. If it has to sit with something, move the whole break by ear and let the snare ring land where it fits.

### How do you squash the Amen break?

One compressor on the bus, detector high-passed above the kick, attack near 10 ms, release set to one sixteenth note at the break’s measured tempo, pushed until the loudest snare reads 6 dB down, then 6 dB of make-up gain. Meter peak and loudness before and after; the drop in the difference between those two is how hard you squashed it.

### Why does my Amen break sound thin after compressing it?

Almost always the attack. Longer than about 10 ms and the stick passes untouched while the drum behind it gets clamped, which leaves a crack with no shell under it. Shorten the attack or take less gain.

### Can you get sued for using the Amen break?

In principle yes: a copyrighted recording that was never licensed for sampling. What has happened for fifty years is that nobody collected, which is a fact about enforcement rather than about permission. That is the record, not legal advice.

### Is the Amen break royalty free?

No. A pack containing a re-recording or a replayed version is a different object from the 1969 master, and only that pack’s own license tells you what you are allowed to do with it.

Vinyl sim is shorthand for a particular kind of squash: dense, slightly crushed drums with the room pushed up under the hits, the way a break sounds once it has been through a sampler. Turning DOSE up makes a drum bus denser rather than louder, because peak level barely moves across the whole range of the knob, and the release reacts to the transient in front of it.

On a loop this dense the only decision left is how much, and DOSE is that decision on one control. The release reacts to the transient in front of it, which on four bars with a ride running underneath is the difference between a wash that surges and a wash that comes up and stays. GAIN and the soft ceiling on the way out hold the top while the block gets denser below it. Run the two measurements from further up the page through it: peak and loudness before, peak and loudness after, and let the subtraction say where to stop.

Four bars, cut so the horn players could rest, on the back of a single nobody was supposed to flip over. In May 2026 the Library of Congress put it in the National Recording Registry.

# Best drum compressor plugins

> The best drum bus compressor plugins, free and paid, which compressor type actually suits drums, and the attack and release numbers that make any of them work.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/best-drum-compressor-plugins/  
Published 2026-09-25, updated 2026-09-26. By Gazillion Industries, who make DRUGS.

---

A loop that filled the room on monitors goes small in the car. The kick and the snare still land, but the hats, the ghost notes and the air between them have gone somewhere. That missing middle is the job of a drum bus compressor, and it is a different job from the one a channel compressor does.

The best drum bus compressor for most records is a clean, fast-acting VCA-style plugin set slow: 2:1 to 4:1, attack 10 to 30 ms, release 150 to 300 ms, pulling 2 to 4 dB on the loudest hits, with a sidechain high-pass near 100 Hz so the kick stops steering the whole kit. Free covers that. DRUGS is ours, free, and does the job from one control called DOSE, timing underneath rather than on the face.

## The short version

- **What we would put on the bus**: DRUGS — ours, free, one knob called DOSE

- **Best type of compressor for drum bus**: VCA — fast, predictable, stays out of the way

- **Starting point, dialing it yourself**: 4:1, 20 ms attack, 200 ms release, 3 dB of gain reduction

- **Sidechain high-pass**: 80–120 Hz, so the kick is not the only thing it hears

- **Best free drum compressor plugin**: ours; then TDR Kotelnikov for control, Klanghelm DC1A for character

- **The real fork**: control, character, or the decision already made

Everything below is the reasoning, the numbers, and an audition test that takes ten minutes and settles the argument faster than a month of forum reading.

## What a drum bus compressor does that a channel compressor does not

A channel compressor listens to one drum and controls that drum. A drum bus compressor listens to all of them summed and controls the sum. The difference sounds administrative and it is the whole category.

When the detector sees the whole kit, every loud element pulls everything else down with it for as long as the gain stays reduced. The kick lands, the hats duck a fraction of a decibel, the room duck along with them, and the gain walks back up in the gap. That coupling is the effect. Separate hits stop reading as separate recordings and start reading as one performance in one space, because they now share a single moving gain. The reason a [drum bus](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-a-drum-bus/) exists at all is to give you a place to do that.

The second thing it does is raise the floor. Compressing peaks and adding make-up gain lifts everything that was not a peak: the decay of the snare, the bleed in the overheads, the tail of the room. A kit with a high [crest factor](https://gazillionindustries.com/crest-factor/) has a lot of space under the peaks, and a bus compressor is the cheapest way to fill it. This is why a compressed drum bus reads as bigger and not merely quieter, which is the single most common thing producers report and the thing they cannot get from compressing each drum on its own.

The cost is that the coupling works in both directions. Put a compressor across the bus and the kick now modulates the hats. Whether that reads as groove or as a wobble depends entirely on the release time relative to the tempo, which is the section with the numbers in it.

## Best type of compressor for drum bus: VCA, FET, opto, vari-mu

Four gain-cell families turn up in the marketing copy for nearly every compressor plugin sold, and on drums they are not interchangeable. What follows is what each one does to a kit, in the order most useful to you.

### VCA

A voltage-controlled amplifier design gives you fast, accurate, fully adjustable timing. The attack can be genuinely fast, the release can be genuinely long, and the gain change tracks the control voltage without much of its own opinion. On a drum bus this is usually what you want. You are shaping timing, and timing is the one thing a VCA topology will give you exactly. Most digital bus compressors, including the console-style ones everybody reaches for, sit in this family. If you only ever own one, own this.

### FET

A field-effect transistor design is very fast and it distorts on the way. That distortion is the appeal. Attack times in the microseconds mean a FET-style plugin can grab a stick hit before the stick has finished, which flattens the transient and pushes the body forward, and the harmonic mess it adds while doing so reads as aggression. On a snare channel it is frequently the best compressor plugin for snare drum duty you will find. Across a whole bus it can be glorious or it can be a smear, depending on how much low end is hitting the detector.

### Opto

An optical design uses a light source and a light-dependent resistor, and the resistor takes its time. Attack and release are slow, program-dependent and largely out of your hands, which makes an opto plugin a poor first choice on a drum bus: drums are a timing problem and this is the topology with the least timing control. It works as a second, gentler stage catching long-term drift, or on a room mic you want to swell rather than snap.

### Vari-mu

A variable-mu design uses tubes whose gain falls as signal rises, so the ratio increases with level rather than sitting at a fixed number. Soft at the bottom, firm at the top. On a drum bus this is the least obvious compression of the four, because the onset is gradual and there is no single point where the sound changes. Wrong tool for a snare that is 6 dB too loud. Right tool when the bus is already balanced and you want density with no visible seam.

- **Punch and control**: VCA

- **Aggression and grit**: FET

- **Slow swell, no timing control**: opto

- **Density with no seam**: vari-mu

One caution about the taxonomy. Two plugins wearing the same topology label can be further apart than two wearing different ones. Use the family names to narrow the shortlist, then use your ears.

## The fork: control or character

Every argument about the best drum compressor plugin collapses into one question, and almost nobody asks it out loud. Do you want the compressor to control the drums, or do you want it to change them?

Control means the gain moves and nothing else does. Transients survive, the tone at the output matches the tone at the input, and nulling the processed signal against the dry one at matched level leaves only level. Transparent bus compression is a real engineering target and a hard one, and the plugins that hit it advertise the fact.

Character means the compressor adds harmonics, shifts the low end, softens the top, or all three, whether you asked or not. It is why a bus compressor can improve a loop while doing almost no gain reduction at all, which is a hint that the gain reduction was never the point on that particular plugin.

There is a third branch, and it is the one most people are actually on: you want neither decision, you want the drums fixed. A plugin built for one bus can make the control-or-character call once, at the factory, and hand you a single knob. That is a real trade and the section below puts it first, because it is what we build.

Neither of the first two is better. What matters is knowing which one you reached for, because they fail in opposite ways. A transparent compressor asked to add life will do nothing and you will keep turning it up until the kit is flat. A character compressor asked to control a wild bus will color everything long before it has caught the peaks, and you will end up with a loud, busy, still-uneven drum bus. Half the plugins people buy are the right plugin for the other job.

Check the changelog on the maker's page before a free compressor becomes load-bearing — Kotelnikov's carries its version history openly. ## Attack and release against tempo, with the numbers

Attack decides whether the drums punch. Release decides whether the bus breathes in time. Both are tempo problems, and the maddening part is that the same numbers give opposite results at different tempos, which is why copied settings so rarely survive the trip.

A quarter note lasts 60,000 divided by the tempo, in milliseconds. Three worked examples, with the sixteenth note included because on most drum programming the sixteenth is the shortest gap the compressor has to recover in.

- **90 bpm**: quarter 667 ms, eighth 333 ms, sixteenth 167 ms

- **140 bpm**: quarter 429 ms, eighth 214 ms, sixteenth 107 ms

- **170 bpm**: quarter 353 ms, eighth 176 ms, sixteenth 88 ms

Set the release so the gain is back near zero before the next hit you care about. At 90 bpm on a sparse boom-bap loop, the next hit you care about is usually the eighth, so 200 to 300 ms lands cleanly inside 333 ms and the compressor is idle again when the snare arrives. At 170 bpm with sixteenth hats, 200 ms means the gain never gets back up at all and the whole bus sits permanently pulled down, which is the flat, lifeless result people blame on the plugin. Same setting, opposite outcome, and the only thing that changed was the tempo.

Attack works the other way. Under about 3 ms and the compressor catches the stick itself, which kills the crack; the plugins that do this on purpose are the FET-style ones, and the grit they add is the compensation. At 10 to 30 ms the [transient](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-a-transient/) is already through the door before the gain moves, so the hit stays sharp and the body behind it gets squeezed. If your drums lost their punch the moment you engaged the compressor, attack is the first thing to check and it is right roughly nine times out of ten.

The sidechain high-pass is the control nobody mentions and it changes more than either of the above. Without it, a drum bus compressor is very nearly a kick-triggered ducker, because the kick carries most of the energy and the detector is an energy detector. High-pass the detector at 80 to 120 Hz and the snare and the hats start contributing to the gain decision. The kit suddenly sounds like a kit instead of a pump. Set it by sweeping up until the gain reduction meter stops moving in perfect lockstep with the kick, then leave it there. The full control-by-control walk is in [drum bus compressor settings](https://gazillionindustries.com/drum-bus-compressor-settings/).

## Best parallel drum bus compressor setup

Parallel compression lets you have the compressed sound without giving up the dynamics, which on drums is close to having it both ways. You keep the dry kit at full transient, and you blend a heavily compressed copy underneath it that carries the room, the decay and the density.

The old method is a send to a return track with a compressor on it. The modern method is a Mix or Dry/Wet control on the compressor itself, which every plugin named above has, and which is better in one specific way: the dry and wet paths are sample-aligned inside the plugin, so there is no chance of a delay-compensation mismatch smearing the transient. If you have ever set up parallel drums on a send and found the result oddly soft, that is the usual culprit.

Settings for the parallel copy are the inverse of the ones above. Go hard: 8:1 or higher, the fastest attack the plugin has, a short release, 10 dB or more of gain reduction. The point of the parallel path is to be squashed into a single dense block, because you are going to hide it under a dry signal that already has all the punch. Then bring it up from silence until the kit thickens, and stop about 2 dB before the point where it sounds good on its own. Our longer piece on [parallel compression](https://gazillionindustries.com/parallel-compression/) covers the routing in both directions.

On DRUGS that control is **MIX**, and there is no latency anywhere in the path, so the dry stays sample-aligned with the wet at every setting and parallel compression will not comb-filter on you. Take DOSE most of the way up, then pull MIX back until the dry kit is still the first thing you hear. The shot below is DOSE 95 with MIX at 45, which is an ordinary place to land on a break.

**DOSE 95, MIX 45.** Crushed underneath, dry on top — parallel without a send.

One check that saves an hour: listen to the parallel bus in mono. A heavily compressed drum copy is where stereo width problems become audible first, because compression raises the correlated and the uncorrelated content together and the room mics are the uncorrelated part. If the kit hollows out when you sum, pull the parallel level down before you start reaching for width tools.

## Best compressor plugin for kick drum and snare drum

Channel compression on individual drums is a repair, not a default. Before you put a compressor on a kick, ask what is wrong with it, because the answer is often a level automation problem or a sample choice problem and a compressor will make both worse.

When it is the right tool on a kick, you want the opposite of bus settings. Fast release, so the gain is back before the next kick; medium attack, 5 to 15 ms, to let the beater click through; a low ratio and shallow reduction, because a kick has little dynamic range to start with and squashing it makes it shorter rather than bigger. Any VCA design does this cleanly. A kick that needs to be bigger rather than steadier is a [saturation](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-saturate-drums/) job.

Snares are where channel compression earns its place, and where the best compressor plugin for snare drum question has a real answer: a fast FET-style design. The range between the hard hits and the ghost notes is enormous, and a fast compressor with a moderate release brings the ghosts up into audibility, which is most of what makes a programmed snare sound played. Expect 6 dB or more of reduction, far too much on the bus and normal on one drum. Watch the decay: too short a release and the tail flutters, too long and the ghosts never arrive.

Then take both off and listen to the bus again. Individual compression that sounded like an improvement in solo frequently disappears in the mix, and every stage you leave in is a stage the bus compressor has to work around.

## What you already have installed

The stock options are better than their reputation. What follows is what each one is, in a sentence, rather than a course in driving it.

Glue Compressor is the console-style bus compressor built with Cytomic, described above. Drum Buss is a different animal: an analog-style drum processor with a fixed compressor on a toggle — Ableton describe it as fast attack, medium release, moderate ratio with ample make-up — followed by three distortion stages, soft waveshaping, medium limiting and hard clipping with a bass boost. Drum Buss is a character box with a compressor inside, so treat it as such.

**Logic Pro** ships one Compressor with main, output and side chain parameter pages, and it is entirely capable of holding a drum bus.

**FL Studio** has Fruity Limiter, which Image-Line document as a single-band compressor with sidechain, a limiter and a gate in one plugin, with COMP and LIMIT tabs and a signal path running input, compressor, gain, limiter, saturation, output. That saturation stage on the end makes it a reasonable one-stop drum bus. Maximus, the Fruity Compressor and the Fruity Multiband Compressor sit alongside it.

In every case the chain position matters as much as the plugin, and [what order drum bus plug-ins go in](https://gazillionindustries.com/drum-bus-chain-order/) is its own question.

Every number on this page is a decision somebody has to make. If you would rather not make them, [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html) is free, it is one knob, and the decisions are already in it.

## The ten-minute audition test

This settles which compressor belongs on your bus faster than any review, including this one. Do it with a loop you know intimately, not with a demo file. Start with ours, because it costs nothing and steps two, five, six and seven collapse into one knob; steps three, nine and ten are the ones that decide anything.

- Load the compressor on the drum bus with all other bus processing bypassed.

- Set ratio 4:1, attack 20 ms, release 200 ms, and lower the threshold until the meter reads 3 dB on the loudest hits.

- Adjust the output gain until bypassed and engaged measure the same loudness.

- Bypass and engage five times while listening to the hats and the room, not the kick.

- Set the attack to its fastest value and listen for the stick going soft.

- Return the attack to 20 ms and shorten the release until the bus pumps, then back off until it stops.

- Engage the sidechain high-pass and sweep it from 20 Hz to 200 Hz while watching the gain reduction meter.

- Drive the threshold down to 10 dB of reduction for fifteen seconds to hear the plugin's character with the politeness removed.

- Return to 3 dB, rematch the loudness, and play the loop on a phone speaker.

- Keep the plugin only if step nine sounded better than the bypass.

Step three is the one people skip and it invalidates everything after it. Louder wins every blind comparison for the first few seconds, and an unmatched level is responsible for a large share of the moments where a plugin sounds transformative in a demo and ordinary in a session. A [VU meter](https://gazillionindustries.com/vu-meter/) or any loudness meter across the bus makes the match a five-second job.

## What it costs

Bus compression is not free in any sense except the price. Four costs, plainly.

It takes away dynamic range, and dynamic range is what makes a fill feel like a fill. A bus squeezed hard enough to sound huge in an eight-bar loop turns relentless across three minutes, which you cannot hear while working on the loop and can hear instantly on the arrangement.

It moves the low end. Any compressor with a full-range detector is being driven mostly by the kick, so the perceived balance between the kick and everything else shifts as you increase the amount. The high-pass helps and does not eliminate it.

It makes mistakes further back harder to fix. Once the bus is glued, the individual drums are no longer independent, and a snare that needed to come down 2 dB now takes the whole kit with it when you move it. Balance first, compress second.

And it competes with the limiter at the end of the chain. Every decibel of crest factor you remove on the drum bus is a decibel the master [limiter](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-use-a-limiter/) does not get to remove, which is fine until both are working hard and the record stops moving at all.

## Questions people ask

### So what do I actually put on the drum bus?

Ours, first, because finding out costs nothing. DRUGS on the bus, DOSE up until the room comes forward under the hits, GAIN to match the bypassed level, and listen on a phone. If ten minutes of that leaves you wanting the timing controls back in your own hands, everything named on this page is still there and you now know which one does what.

### What is the best drum bus compressor plugin overall?

For a drum bus specifically, ours, and it is free. Past that it is a clean VCA-style bus compressor with a sidechain high-pass: TDR Kotelnikov is the strongest free option for control and Cytomic The Glue at $99 is the reference for the console-style sound. Either way the setting matters more than the purchase — a 20 ms attack and a release tuned to the tempo will do more for your drums than anything in this category costs.

### What is the best type of compressor for a drum bus?

VCA, in almost every case, because a drum bus is a timing problem and VCA designs give you the most accurate control over timing. FET when you want the compressor to add aggression, vari-mu when the bus is already balanced and you want density with no obvious onset. Opto is the weakest choice here, since its attack and release are largely fixed and slow.

### What do people on Reddit recommend for a drum bus compressor?

The recurring recommendations are a console-style bus compressor for glue, a fast FET-style one for parallel, and the point that most people are using too much. That last one is right. The threads are also full of purchases made to solve problems that turned out to be an attack time, so read them for the technique and be skeptical of the shopping list.

### Is there a genuinely good free drum compressor plugin?

Several, and one of them is ours. DRUGS is free for Mac and Windows, one control, built for this bus and nothing else. TDR Kotelnikov gives you separate release controls for peak and RMS content plus a sidechain filter and a delta preview, which is more control than most paid plugins offer. Klanghelm DC1A covers the character end in two knobs. Kilohearts Essentials is free with an account and includes a compressor, a limiter and a transient shaper. None of these are crippled trial versions.

### How much gain reduction should a drum bus compressor do?

Two to four decibels on the loudest hits for glue you feel rather than hear. Four to six is obvious and still musical on drums. Past six you are making an effect, which is a legitimate choice as long as you made it on purpose. If the meter never returns to zero you have stopped compressing and started limiting, and [the difference matters](https://gazillionindustries.com/limiter-vs-compressor/).

### Should I use one compressor on the drum bus or one on each drum?

Start with the bus. It is the stage that makes separate hits sound like one kit and it is the one you would miss if it vanished. Add channel compression only where a specific drum has a specific problem, and take it off again if the bus already solved it. Two stages of light compression usually beat one stage of heavy, but three stages is where mixes go to die.

### Why do my drums sound worse after I compress them?

In order of likelihood: the attack is too fast and is eating the transients; the level is not matched so you are comparing loud against quiet; the release is longer than the gap between hits so the gain never recovers; or there is no sidechain high-pass and the kick is ducking the entire kit. Work through those four in that order and the fourth one rarely survives.
