# The Alchemist

> How The Alchemist works: the ASR-10 years, swing at 62 percent, quantizing one element and leaving the rest, and the truth about the drumless records.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/alchemist/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

A producer who made his reputation on hard New York drums spent the last decade making records with almost no drums at all, and became more influential doing it. The swing setting he works at is a number you can type into your own sampler.

Alan Maman, who produces as The Alchemist, was born in 1977 in Beverly Hills, became Mobb Deep's DJ and in-house producer in New York, and has spent the years since making collaborative albums with one rapper at a time: Alfredo with Freddie Gibbs, The Price of Tea in China with Boldy James, Haram with Armand Hammer, Covert Coup with Curren$y. He worked on an Ensoniq ASR-10 for the whole of the nineties, moved to the MPC and Pro Tools later, and works fast enough that he does not bother naming his files.

## The short version

- **Born**: 1977, Beverly Hills

- **First machine**: Ensoniq ASR-10, through the nineties and beyond

- **Now**: MPC hardware into Pro Tools

- **Swing**: 62 or 63 percent, his stated comfort zone

- **Build**: two bars, then four, then eight, then sixteen

- **Known for**: one-rapper albums, and rap that often has no drums

## The ASR-10 years

He used an Ensoniq ASR-10 as his main machine for a very long time, well past the point where it was current. His own account of the constraint is the useful part: the sampler gave him only a handful of tracks to work with, and he was still making records on it for major artists years after everyone else had moved to computers. Alongside it, a Korg Triton, which he has credited with beats that were mostly empty and still hit.

That is the same lesson as every other producer worth studying: the limitation was not something he tolerated, it was the thing that made the records sound the way they do. Eight tracks means every decision is a subtraction.

## The numbers he works at

Two specifics worth stealing, both his.

**Swing at 62 or 63 percent.** That is his stated comfort zone, and it lines up with the setting the designer of the MPC recommends for a loosened, relaxed feel. Anyone can type it into a groove control tonight. See [the creation of the MPC](https://gazillionindustries.com/mpc-creation/) for where that number comes from and what it actually does to the sixteenths.

**Quantize one element, leave the rest loose.** Rather than a beat that is all on the grid or all off it, he locks one part and lets the others sit where they land. That is the same principle a lot of people attribute to [J Dilla](https://gazillionindustries.com/j-dilla/), and it is a much more practical description than turning quantize off entirely.

## How he builds one

His arrangement method is almost embarrassingly simple and it is the reason his beats go somewhere. Start with two bars. Make it four. Make it eight. Make it sixteen. He describes it as building a race course for a driver: the rapper is going to drive through it, so it needs corners at predictable intervals and it needs to change often enough that nobody falls asleep at the wheel.

For chopping he leans on mute groups, so one chop cuts off the last, which is what stops a chopped loop turning into a wash of overlapping tails.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) makes plugins for exactly this speed of working: a knob, a result, and back to the next one.

## The drums question

He is the producer most associated with drumless rap, and the story is more interesting than a style choice. He has said that he started wanting to appeal to people who do not care about snares, and separately described the drumless approach as necessity becoming the mother of invention.

It is worth being accurate about the limits of that, though: a lot of his published instruction shows a producer who often starts with drums and builds outward. The honest version is that he has both modes, and that the records people call drumless are a deliberate subtraction from someone who knows exactly what he is removing.

## How the beats reach rappers

In bulk, and remotely. He sends batches and waits to see what moves somebody's pen, and he auditions his own beats by putting other people's vocals over them to hear whether they hold. On the most productive of his partnerships he has put his hit rate around eighty or ninety percent, which tells you the batches are not speculative: they are aimed.

That is also the practical explanation for the one-rapper album format he has made his own. If most of what you send a particular artist works, you may as well make the whole record together.

## Questions people ask

### What equipment does The Alchemist use?

An Ensoniq ASR-10 for most of his career, a Korg Triton alongside it, and Akai MPC hardware into Pro Tools more recently. He has credited another producer with teaching him much of what he does in Pro Tools.

### What swing does The Alchemist use?

He has named 62 or 63 percent as his comfort zone, which is close to the setting the MPC's designer recommends for a relaxed, loosened feel rather than a full triplet swing.

### How does The Alchemist arrange a beat?

Two bars, then four, then eight, then sixteen, building a structure for the rapper to move through. He quantizes one element and leaves the others where they fall.

### Why do his beats have no drums?

He has said he wanted to reach listeners who do not care about snares, and has described the approach as necessity turning into invention. He is perfectly capable of hard drums and often starts with them; the drumless records are a choice.

**DOSE 12.** Most of the time the useful setting is far lower than it looks.

We make [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html). DOSE 12. Most of the time the useful setting is far lower than it looks.

## What to take from it

Set your swing to 62. Quantize one thing and leave the rest alone. Build two bars into sixteen rather than looping two bars for three minutes. And consider what the beat sounds like with the drums muted, because one of the most in-demand producers of the last decade built a second career on that exact question.

Eight tracks on a sampler nobody else was still using, and a catalog most producers with unlimited tracks would trade for.

# Best lofi VST plugins

> The four lofi plugins we make, sorted by the job each does in a chain: bandwidth and grain, tape and transport, speed and pitch, and drum bus density.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/best-lofi-vst/  
Published 2026-09-25, updated 2026-09-25. By Gazillion Industries.

---

Four lofi plugins on the master, and at midnight in headphones the loop sounded properly aged. In the car the next morning it was a quiet mix with the top cut off. Nothing in the chain was wrong; nothing in it was doing a different job from anything else in it.

Straight answer, and the conflict of interest first: the four plugins on this page are the four we make. A lofi chain has four jobs — bandwidth and grain, the medium and its transport, speed and pitch instability, density on the drum bus. F(ilter)12 does the first, TRIPLE OG the second, SKRUU the third, DRUGS the fourth and DRUGS is free. Most people need two of the four.

## The short version

- **Bandwidth and grain**: F(ilter)12 — filter and 12 bit crush on one face, $49, DRUGS included

- **The medium**: TRIPLE OG — cassette tape simulation with a playable transport, $29

- **Speed and pitch**: SKRUU — varispeed, with pitch and time on separate knobs, $29

- **Drum density**: DRUGS — one knob on the drum bus, free, Mac and Windows

- **Start with**: the job your loop is failing at, not the plugin with the best demo

- **You may already own**: a bitcrusher, a filter, a warp mode and a bus compressor

## Why a search for the best lofi VST gives you six answers

Lofi is four kinds of damage and they do not substitute for each other. Bandwidth and grain: the top goes, and the quiet detail gets coarse rather than smooth. The medium: noise under the music, saturation that arrives gradually, a machine that was never steady. Speed: pitch and time that wander, because nothing mechanical holds a rate exactly. Density: drums pressed together until the bus reads as one instrument instead of four channels.

Stack three plugins that all do the first job and you get a duller track at the same address. That is the usual reason a hunt for the best lofi VST plugins ends with six of them on the master and a mix that still sounds like a modern export with a filter over it. The ear is not counting plugins. It is looking for evidence that the sound went through something.

So here is the disclosure in plain words. We make all four of these. This page is our shelf, not a survey of the market, and you should read it the way you read any manufacturer describing its own products. What we can do is tell you which job each one takes, what it refuses to do, and which free tool already covers part of it. Some of those paragraphs are an argument against buying, and they are in here on purpose.

## Bandwidth and grain: F(ilter)12

The first job is subtraction with a texture attached. A plain low-pass makes a track quieter at the top and nothing else happens; an old sampled signal loses its top *and* picks up grain in the quiet parts *and* gets a metallic edge from content folding back down out of range. Three separate mechanisms, and the reason a bitcrusher on its own usually sounds broken is that it only supplies one of them.

F(ilter)12 is a 12 bit sauce filter for Mac and Windows, $49, in AU, VST3 and standalone, with DRUGS included. The **CRUSH PAIR** holds the two controls that matter here: **SAMPLE RATE** steps the rate down, so the top disappears and what used to live above the new rate folds back into the audible range at unrelated frequencies; **BIT** coarsens the steps the wave is measured in, so quiet detail rounds off and picks up an edge. Twelve bits is the clean end of the travel. It only goes down from there.

Behind the pair sits the filter, which is why the two are on one face. **POSITION** is the big knob, **SLOPE** sets how steeply it falls, and **DIRTY** changes its manners. There are five **CUTOFF SHAPE** options and six **Q SHAPE** options, with **DRIVE**, **RESO**, **Q** and **MIX** underneath. **AURA** sits over the top, and the visualizer along the bottom draws what the crush and the filter are doing to the spectrum while you move them. Rate reduction throws debris upward; the filter is what sweeps it. Put them in the wrong order and the result is harsh instead of old.

[F(ilter)12](https://gazillionindustries.com/f12.html) is the one to look at if the complaint about your loop is that it sounds too clean and too wide awake. Twelve bits down to four, five filter shapes, six resonance shapes, and a picture of the damage while you do it. There's a demo on the page.

**4 bit at 8 kHz.** Bits make it grainy, the rate makes it clang.

**What it does not do.** No noise floor. No hiss, no crackle, no room. No speed movement of any kind, so a loop that is stiff will still be stiff at four bits. No compression on its own, though DRUGS comes with it. And it is an effect, so it will not hand you a sound the way an instrument library does. If your problem is that the arrangement is thin rather than clean, this will not fix it.

**What you already have.** Every major host ships a bitcrusher and a filter, and in ten minutes you can put them in series and hear most of this category for nothing. What the stock pair tends to lack is a filter worth sweeping after the crush, and any view of what the aliasing is doing. Start there anyway. [Bitcrushing explained](https://gazillionindustries.com/bitcrushing-explained/) and [what aliasing is](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-aliasing-in-audio/) cover the mechanism, and [what 12 bit sounds like](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-does-12-bit-sound-like/) is the audition.

## The medium and its transport: TRIPLE OG

The second job is the thing the music was recorded onto. A medium contributes four signatures at once, which is why one medium plugin tends to do more work than three specialists: reduced bandwidth, a noise floor that sits under the quiet parts, saturation that comes in gradually rather than as a wall, and a speed that never holds perfectly still. Those four arriving together is what the ear reads as age.

TRIPLE OG is our cassette tape simulation, $29, Mac and Windows, AU, VST3 and standalone. **TONE** sets playback brightness and **DRIVE** the thickness. **AGE** runs from nought to sixty years and makes the tape darker, noisier and less steady as it climbs, which is one control instead of three. **HISS** is a continuous broadband bed, partly decorrelated across the channels so it survives a fold to mono. **WOW FLUT** is the speed instability.

The transport is the half almost nothing else offers. **SLAM** stops the tape and returns it in sync, so the beat is where it should be when the machine comes back. **SCRUB** runs the head backward and springs home. **CATCH** drags, then sprints to catch up. Those are performance moves rather than settings, and they are the reason a lot of people searching for the best lofi tape VST end up wanting a machine rather than a saturation curve.

[TRIPLE OG](https://gazillionindustries.com/tripleog.html) covers three of the four lofi jobs in one pass — bandwidth with TONE and AGE, the noise floor with HISS, and the speed movement with WOW FLUT and the transport. If you are only ever going to own one of ours, most people should own this one. There's a demo on the page.

**AGE reads in years** because that is what the quantity is. Here it is set to 22.

**What it does not do.** No bit reduction and no rate reduction, so the digital half of the lofi sound is not in here. No filter shapes to choose between, and no resonance to sweep. Pitch and time are locked together the way they are on a tape machine, so it cannot hold a length while it moves a note. It also will not press your drums together; that is a different job and it is further down this page.

**What you already have.** Tape-style saturation ships in most hosts, and it will give you the thickness and some of the top-end softening. What stock devices almost never give you is instability you can play by hand. [Wow and flutter](https://gazillionindustries.com/wow-and-flutter/) explains the movement, [tape hiss](https://gazillionindustries.com/tape-hiss/) the floor, and [how to make music sound like cassette](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-music-sound-like-cassette/) puts the whole chain in order.

## Speed and pitch instability: SKRUU

The third job is the one people leave out, and it is the one that carries the most. A track can be bandwidth-limited and noisy and still read as a modern recording with damage applied, because it is metronomically rigid. Older equipment could not hold a rate exactly. Half a percent of drift over a bar is inaudible as pitch and completely audible as age.

SKRUU is our varispeed pitch and time stretch plugin, $29, in VST3, AU and standalone on Mac and Windows. **PITCH** and **TIME** move independently, so the note and the length are two decisions rather than one: lock either and play the other. Because the offset is a change in playback rate rather than a splice, there is no grain window to hear on a transient. **ELASTIC** makes the knob sprung — move it, let go, and it runs home — with **SLOPE** choosing the return shape out of sixteen. **SAMPLING GRADE** steps the rate down when a copy should not share the original's bandwidth: LO-FI 1 runs at 7.81 kHz against a base of 31.25 kHz, and LO-FI 2 runs at 3.9 kHz.

The everyday use is smaller than the demos suggest. Two copies of a keys part, one nudged up by a few cents and one down, and the width is built out of speed rather than a stereo widener. A sprung dip on the last beat of a four bar loop, so the phrase arrives back slightly late and then corrects. A vocal sent to LO-FI 1 for one line, so that line sounds like it came off a different machine.

[SKRUU](https://gazillionindustries.com/skruu.html) is the one for the complaint nobody can name: the loop is dirty enough and still feels typed in rather than played. Pitch and time on separate knobs, sixteen return shapes, and a sampling grade that drops the bandwidth of a copy without touching the original. There's a demo on the page.

**SAMPLING GRADE at LO-FI 1.** 7.81 kHz rather than 31.25.

**What it does not do.** No noise, no hiss, no crackle. No saturation and no compression. No filter with shapes to pick from. Used alone on a clean source it will make that source move, and the source will still be clean while it moves. It is also the easiest of the four to overdo: enough drift to shift a downbeat reads as a mistake rather than as tape.

**What you already have.** Every host has some route to varispeed, and most people never use it. Ableton Live has the Repitch warp mode. Logic Pro has Varispeed at the project level and Flex Time on the region. FL Studio will resample a channel when you move its pitch. Reaper changes item playback rate with pitch preservation switched off. [Varispeed in every DAW](https://gazillionindustries.com/varispeed-in-every-daw/) has the exact route for each, and [what varispeed is](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-varispeed/) covers why it sounds different from a pitch shifter.

## Density on the drum bus: DRUGS, which is free

The fourth job is the one that decides whether a lofi beat has any weight. Dusty drums that are also weak are the standard failure of this genre, because every process above removes energy: the filter takes the top, the tape softens the transient, the speed movement smears the attack. Something has to put the hits back together at the end, and on a drum bus that something is compression.

DRUGS is a one knob bus compressor for drums, free, Mac and Windows. **DOSE** is the compression, and it moves the transfer curve, the knee, the attack and the release together, so a drum bus gets denser rather than louder as you turn it up. The release is adaptive: a hit gets the shorter time so gain recovers inside the gap, and sustained material gets the longer one so it holds still. **MIX** is dry/wet with zero latency, which gives you parallel without a send. **GAIN** adds 5 dB after the compressor, and **LIMIT** is a soft ceiling at −0.3 dBFS on the output, transparent below about −0.9 dBFS. One knob, and nothing underneath it for you to set.

[DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html) is free and it is the last stage of a lofi chain rather than the first. Put it across the drum bus after the character plugins, not before them, so it is gluing the damaged version rather than the clean one. There's a demo on the page.

**DOSE 88.** It dives on each hit and takes the bar to come back.

**What it does not do.** No tone controls, no saturation section, no filter, no noise. It has one macro and a mix knob, which is the whole design and also the whole limitation: if you want a specific attack time on a specific snare, this is the wrong tool and a full featured compressor is the right one. One more thing worth saying out loud, since we would rather you heard it from us than found it in a session. Turning DOSE down is not a way back to the source. At the bottom of its travel the plugin is still in the signal path and still working on the sound, so when you want an honest before and after, bypass it at the host rather than backing the knob off.

**What you already have.** A bus compressor, in every host on the market. Ableton Live has the Glue Compressor, Logic Pro has Compressor with selectable circuits, FL Studio has Fruity Limiter in its compressor mode, Reaper has ReaComp. Any of them will do this job if you know the settings, which are in [drum bus compressor settings](https://gazillionindustries.com/drum-bus-compressor-settings/) and [how to compress drums](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-compress-drums/). DRUGS exists because most people do not want to learn four controls to make drums denser, and because free removes the argument.

## What none of the four will do for you

Four gaps, stated plainly, because the fastest way to waste money in this category is to buy an effect when you needed an instrument.

**No instrument.** Lofi keys, lofi guitars, dusty drum kits: those are sample libraries recorded through the character, and none of ours is one. An effect improves what you already played. A library gives you something to play. If your loop is boring, a search for the best lofi effect VST is the wrong search.

**No crackle and no field noise.** TRIPLE OG gives you a broadband hiss bed. It does not give you needle noise, surface pops, rain, a coffee shop or a cassette door closing. A [vinyl sim](https://gazillionindustries.com/vinyl-sim-plugin/) or a noise library covers that, and a looped noise file in a spare track covers it for nothing.

**No space.** None of the four is a reverb or a delay. A great deal of what people hear as lofi is actually a small dark room around a dry sample, and no amount of bit reduction substitutes for it.

**No loudness.** BEEFY, our saturation and soft clipping plugin at $19, is not a lofi tool and we would rather say so than sell it to you sideways. It makes things bigger and more present, which is the opposite journey from the one this page is about. It belongs after the lofi chain, or on a different record.

## What you probably already own, per host

Read this section before the price section. It is easier to judge whether a paid plugin is worth it once you have heard the free version of the same idea in your own project.

**Ableton Live.** Redux does bit depth and sample rate. Auto Filter does the filter, with an LFO if you want movement. Saturator and Vinyl Distortion cover the dirt, Erosion adds noise, and the Glue Compressor handles the drum bus. Repitch warp mode is your varispeed. That is four of the four jobs, at a lower ceiling.

**Logic Pro.** Bitcrusher and AutoFilter for the first job, Tape Delay and the vintage console channel strips for flavor, Compressor on the bus, Varispeed at project level and Flex Time per region for speed. Logic is the best equipped of the big hosts here out of the box.

**FL Studio.** Fruity Squeeze covers bit depth and resampling together with a filter, Fruity Filter does the sweeps, Fruity Limiter in compressor mode does the bus, Edison handles stretching, and moving a sampler channel's pitch with resampling on gives you the speed change.

**Pro Tools.** Lo-Fi is one plugin covering bit depth, sample rate, saturation and noise, which makes it the single most useful stock device in this list. Dyn3 Compressor for the bus, Elastic Audio for time.

**Reaper.** ReaComp on the bus, ReaEQ and the JS effects for filtering and degradation, and item playback rate with pitch preservation off for varispeed. Least polished, most complete.

## The ten minute audition, in order

Do this before you buy anything, including ours. It is the test we use, and it is designed to stop you buying the plugin that was simply louder in the demo.

- Bounce eight bars of your loop to an audio file at the project sample rate and work on the file, not the live arrangement.

- Set the monitoring level once and do not touch it again until the test is finished.

- Play the eight bars twice with nothing inserted, and write down one word for what is missing: dull, clean, stiff or thin.

- Load only the plugin that matches that word. Dull means bandwidth, clean means the medium, stiff means speed, thin means density.

- Turn its main control up until the effect is obviously too much, then back it off until you stop hearing the plugin and start hearing the change.

- Trim the output until the loudest bar reads within 0.5 dB of the original bounce.

- Bypass the plugin at the host, not at its own mix control, and switch back and forth four times.

- Keep it only if the bypassed version now sounds worse. If it does not, remove it and go back to step three.

- Repeat once with a second plugin. Never more than two in a single pass.

- Play the result on a phone speaker before you add a third.

Step six is the one people skip and it is the one that decides the outcome. Every process on this page changes loudness, louder wins almost every blind comparison, and an unmatched A/B is a test that cannot fail.

## What all four cost, and what they cost you

In money: DRUGS is free. TRIPLE OG is $29 and SKRUU is $29. F(ilter)12 is $49 with DRUGS included, so buying F(ilter)12 first and adding the other two comes to $107 for the set. Nobody needs the set on day one.

In sound, the costs are more interesting, and each one is real.

**Bandwidth and grain cost you presence.** Everything you crush and filter moves backward in the mix. Do it to all four elements and the record has no front row.

**The medium costs you the transient.** Tape softens attacks, which is most of why it sounds friendly, and it is also why a heavily aged drum bus stops cutting through on a laptop speaker. That is what the compression at the end is for.

**Speed movement costs you tuning.** Anything you drift is now slightly out with everything you did not drift. Bass lines and sustained keys expose this first; drums and short chops hide it.

**Density costs you dynamics.** A drum bus squeezed hard reads as loud and stops reading as performed. The fix is the mix control rather than a smaller dose, since parallel keeps the peaks and adds the body underneath.

## What the threads get right

The best lofi VST Reddit threads land on the same three pieces of advice, and all three are correct. Buy fewer plugins. Learn one deeply. Your DAW already does most of this.

The fourth thing those threads tend to agree on is worth repeating too: the sound people are chasing usually came from a specific sampler with specific limits, not from a plugin at all, and the honest route is to understand the limit rather than to buy an approximation of it. [How to get an old sampler sound](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-get-an-old-sampler-sound/) goes through what those limits actually were. What the threads are worse at is the free part of the answer, because nobody ever posts to recommend the device already installed in their host.

Where we disagree with the consensus is small but it matters. The advice to pick one plugin and learn it is right about depth and wrong about coverage, because one plugin cannot cover four jobs. Two can cover three of them. Start with a medium plugin and a bus compressor, work at those for a month, and add the others only when you can say in one sentence what is missing.

## Questions people ask

### What is the best lofi VST?

The one that does the job your track is failing at. Dull and wide awake needs bandwidth and grain. Clean and modern needs a medium. Stiff needs speed movement. Weak drums need density. A medium plugin covers the most ground of the four, which is why it is the usual first purchase. The best VST plugins for lofi, taken as a set, are the ones that cover different jobs from each other rather than the ones with the best individual reviews.

### What is the best lofi VST free?

The stock devices in your host, in almost every case. A bitcrusher, a filter, a saturator and a bus compressor ship with every major DAW, and together they cover three of the four jobs. DRUGS is free and handles the fourth. The gap in free tools is speed instability and a transport you can play by hand. [Free VST plugins](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-free-vst-plugins/) has more.

### What is the best VST for lofi drums?

Two plugins in series, in this order: something that damages the sound, then something that glues it. Most best lofi drum VST lists mix sample libraries in with effects, and both of these are effects. The damage is bandwidth, grain or tape. The glue is a bus compressor, and DRUGS does that for nothing. Running the compressor first flattens the dynamics that the character stage needed to work on. [How to make lofi drums](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-lofi-drums/) is the full chain, and [drum bus chain order](https://gazillionindustries.com/drum-bus-chain-order/) covers the order.

### What is the best lofi tape VST?

Look for speed instability and a transport, because saturation on its own is available almost everywhere. A tape plugin that only warms the signal is doing the same job as the saturator already in your host. TRIPLE OG is ours, at $29, with SLAM, SCRUB and CATCH on the face. Others are surveyed in [best lofi plugins](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-lofi-plugins/).

### What is the best VST for lofi hip hop specifically?

Lofi hip hop leans harder on the drum bus than the rest of the genre, because the loops are usually sparse and the drums carry the record. Start with density, then add a medium, then leave it alone. The chain in [how to make lofi beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-lofi-beats/) works for it, and [how to make Dilla type beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-dilla-type-beats/) goes deeper on the timing side.

### What do people on Reddit recommend as the best lofi plugin?

Consistently: fewer plugins, learned properly, plus whatever your DAW already ships. That advice is correct. The part it misses is that one plugin cannot cover bandwidth, medium, speed and density at once, so two well chosen tools beat one deeply learned one in this particular category.

### How many lofi VST plugins do I actually need?

Two, for most people. A medium plugin and a bus compressor will get a clean loop most of the way there, and adding a third before you can name what is still wrong is how chains get to six plugins doing one job. Audition with the ten step test above and stop when the phone speaker agrees with the headphones.

### What order should lofi VST plugins go in?

Speed and pitch first, while the material still has its full bandwidth. Bit and rate reduction next. Filtering after that, so it can sweep the aliasing the rate reduction threw upward. Tape and noise near the end, because the medium is the last thing the sound was recorded onto. Compression last of all, on the bus, gluing the damaged version rather than the clean one. A chain that sounds harsh instead of warm almost always has the filter in front of the crush.

Back in the car. The mix that was quiet with the top cut off had four plugins doing one job between them. Two doing different ones would have survived the drive.

# The Capitol echo chambers

> How the Capitol Records echo chambers work: eight concrete rooms under a Hollywood car park, why they are trapezoidal, and why reverb used to be real estate.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/capitol-echo-chambers/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

Thirty feet under a parking lot in Hollywood there are eight concrete rooms with a speaker at one end and a microphone at the other. They have been in continuous professional use since 1956, they are still bookable, and no plugin on your machine is doing anything they do not do first.

The Capitol echo chambers are eight subterranean reverb rooms beneath the Capitol Records Tower in Los Angeles. Sound from any studio or mastering room in the building is sent down to a speaker inside a chamber, allowed to bounce around the concrete, and picked up again by a microphone, which returns it to the session with up to five seconds of decay on it. Chambers one to four were designed by Les Paul and built with the tower in 1956. Chambers five to eight were added in 1969.

## The short version

- **Where**: 30 feet below the Capitol Tower's parking lot

- **How many**: eight; 1–4 from 1956, 5–8 added in 1969

- **Designed by**: Les Paul, for the original four

- **Shape**: trapezoidal, thick concrete, hard lacquered ceilings

- **Decay**: up to five seconds

- **Method**: speaker at one end, microphone at the other

## Why the shape and the surfaces

Every design decision in those rooms exists to stop the reverb from having a character of its own. Parallel walls produce standing waves, which means certain frequencies ring longer than others and the room imposes a pitch on everything you send it. Trapezoidal rooms have no parallel surfaces, so the reflections scatter rather than stack.

The surfaces do the other half. Thick concrete walls and ceilings finished with a highly reflective hard lacquer absorb almost nothing, which is what buys the long decay: the sound keeps bouncing because nothing in the room is willing to soak it up. A carpeted room with soft walls would give you a short, dull reverb. These give you five seconds of it.

And each chamber was deliberately built to sound different from the others, so the engineer gets a choice rather than a setting.

## The detail that tells you what they were worth

Capitol used to lease the chambers to other studios. United Western Recorders and The Village would send audio down to Hollywood and back over telephone lines, in real time, because it was worth the trouble and the cost to get those specific rooms on their records.

That is the fact to sit with. Before convolution, before plates were common and cheap, the only way to get a great reverb was to own a great space or rent somebody else's down a phone line. Reverb was real estate.

## Two ways to make something bigger

Reverb and saturation solve the same complaint from opposite directions, and knowing which one you need is most of the skill.

A chamber adds *time*. It puts the sound in a space, surrounds it with reflections and makes it feel large because it is taking up more of the second. The cost is clarity: everything you send down there comes back blurred, the gaps between notes fill in, and a dense arrangement turns to mud fast.

Saturation, covered in [its own guide](https://gazillionindustries.com/saturation-explained/), adds *content*. It generates harmonics that were not in the source, which makes a sound denser and more present without adding a millisecond to its length. The cost is space in the spectrum rather than space in time: harmonics stack up in the upper mids and crowd the same range every other instrument wants.

Which is why the classic records made in that building use both, on different things. Strings and voices go to the chamber. The rhythm section mostly does not.

## What happened to them

They are still there and still working, which is genuinely unusual: most of the great purpose-built chambers of that era were demolished, converted or filled in when the real estate became worth more than the reverb. In 2019 Universal Audio released officially licensed software emulations of the four most popular chambers, which is as close as most people will get, and the building itself has been a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument since 2006.

A cassette transport rather than a tape saturator — the machine as well as the medium.

We make [TRIPLE OG](https://gazillionindustries.com/tripleog.html). A cassette transport rather than a tape saturator — the machine as well as the medium.

## What to take from it if you have no concrete

- Use fewer reverbs, and longer ones, on fewer sources. Eight chambers existed so engineers could choose one, not send everything.

- Send rather than insert. The chamber method is a send: the dry signal stays, and a separate wet version returns.

- Keep the low end out of it. Real chambers were fed through the electronics of their day and did not receive much below the low mids.

- Decide per element whether you want time or content: reverb for a voice, saturation for a drum bus.

- Check in mono. Chamber reverb is a mono return in many classic records and it survives summing; a wide modern stereo reverb often does not.

## Questions people ask

### How do the Capitol echo chambers work?

Audio from a studio is played through a speaker inside a sealed concrete room and re-recorded by a microphone at the other end. The signal that returns carries the room's reverberation, which is mixed back in with the dry sound.

### How many echo chambers does Capitol have?

Eight. The first four were designed by Les Paul and built with the tower in 1956; chambers five to eight were added in 1969.

### How long is the reverb in the Capitol chambers?

Up to about five seconds, which is very long for a room of that size and is a product of hard concrete surfaces that absorb almost nothing.

### Can you still use them?

Yes. They remain in use at Capitol Studios and all of the building's rooms have access to them, including the mastering team.

Eight concrete rooms under a car park, rented out over the phone, still working seventy years later. Your reverb plugin has a preset named after them.

# DJ Premier

> How DJ Premier works: sampling into one machine and triggering from another, chops recombined from sections nobody else takes, and the SP-1200 correction.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/dj-premier/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

Thirty years of records that sound like one person made them, built on a sampler with sixty seconds of memory and a drum machine he does not sample with. The technique is documented in his own words and it is stranger than the reputation.

Christopher Martin, who produces as DJ Premier, was born on 21 March 1966 in Houston and became half of Gang Starr with Guru before producing a run of records that defined New York rap in the nineties: Nas, Biggie, Jay-Z, Jeru the Damaja, Mobb Deep, KRS-One, Rakim. His method has two parts people usually get wrong. He splits the job between two machines, sampling into one and triggering from the other, and he builds loops out of fragments rather than lifting bars.

## The short version

- **Born**: 21 March 1966, Houston

- **Group**: Gang Starr, with Guru, who died in 2010

- **Samples into**: an Akai S950, with its 60-second limit

- **Triggers from**: an MPC60, the original, not the MkII

- **Chops**: sections recombined, obvious breaks deliberately skipped

- **Hooks**: scratched, and placed by where the sample lands

## Two machines, one job each

The sentence that explains his whole setup, given to Sound On Sound in 2007: "I don't sample with the MPC60, I just use it to trigger drums. Instead I sample in the S950 and trigger them from the MPC."

The S950 is a rack sampler with about sixty seconds of memory. That constraint is not incidental; it is the reason the chops are short and the reason nothing in his records is a long borrowed passage. The MPC60 is there for its pads and its timing, which is a very deliberate way of dividing the work between a machine that stores sound well and a machine that plays it well. Our piece on [the creation of the MPC](https://gazillionindustries.com/mpc-creation/) covers why that second machine's timing was worth building a workflow around.

His machine lineage, in his own account, runs from a Yamaha drum machine through an E-mu SP-12, an Alesis HR-11 and an Akai S900 to the MPC60, which he bought secondhand from an engineer and adopted around Gang Starr's Daily Operation in 1992.

## The correction

He is routinely described as an SP-1200 producer. He says he never used one: by the time it shipped he had already moved to a different drum machine. The claim appears to have spread from one loosely worded magazine sentence and has been repeated ever since. If you are studying his drum sound, you are studying an S950 and an MPC60, not the machine everyone names.

## How the chops actually work

The best outside description of his sampling comes from Adrian Younge, and it is worth stating precisely because it is the part that cannot be copied by loading a break. Premier takes three or four separate sections from a record and recombines them into a phrase that was never played. He deliberately avoids the obvious break, the part any other producer would take. And he pitches individual chops against each other, which means the melody in the finished loop is frequently not the melody in the source at all — it has been rewritten out of pieces.

That is why his loops feel composed rather than borrowed, and it is also why sample-spotting his records is so difficult. There is often no single bar in the original that sounds like what you are hearing.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) makes plugins for people who work in fragments: commit the chop, print it, keep going.

## The drums, and the quantize question

He answers it directly: "I tend to program my drums, but a lot of the time I'll turn off the 16th notes and I'll play the MPC live, so it sounds like live drumming." Both modes, chosen per record. That is the same answer the honest sources give about every great drum programmer of that era, and it is more useful than either of the slogans people prefer.

## The scratch hooks

The chorus made of cut-up vocal phrases from other records is his signature and it is a DJ's technique rather than a producer's. The selection comes out of a DJ's memory — knowing which record has the word you need — and the placement is decided by where the sample lands against the beat rather than by a plan. It is the one part of his method that genuinely requires having been a working DJ first.

## The room

He worked out of D&D Studios in Manhattan and later owned the room, renaming it. He moved off two-inch tape in 2005 and has worked in Pro Tools since, with a large-format control surface and a fairly plain plugin set. One detail worth knowing because it is unusual: he has described using de-essers as a color rather than as a repair, which is a very specific piece of engineering taste.

On pace, ignore the number you have read. The widely repeated fifteen-minutes-a-beat figure belongs to somebody else describing another producer. Premier's own account of his rate is four days for five or six songs.

## Questions people ask

### What equipment does DJ Premier use?

An Akai S950 for sampling and an Akai MPC60 for triggering and sequencing, with Pro Tools for recording since 2005. He has said explicitly that he does not sample into the MPC.

### Did DJ Premier use the SP-1200?

He says he did not. His own account of his machines goes from a Yamaha drum machine to an E-mu SP-12, then an Alesis HR-11, an Akai S900 and the MPC60.

### How does DJ Premier chop samples?

He takes several separate sections of a record, avoids the obvious break, recombines them into a phrase the original never contained, and pitches individual chops so the resulting melody is partly his own.

### Does DJ Premier quantize?

Sometimes. In his words, he programs his drums, but often turns the sixteenths off and plays the pads live so it sounds like live drumming.

One knob on the drum bus, voiced for breaks rather than for a mix.

We make [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html). One knob on the drum bus, voiced for breaks rather than for a mix.

## What to take from it

The transferable idea is the recombination. Most producers loop the best bar; he takes the parts nobody wants, in three pieces, and builds a phrase that did not exist. It is slower, it is harder, and it is the reason nobody can find his samples. [How to chop samples](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-chop-samples/) has the mechanics, and [how to flip a sample](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-flip-a-sample/) has the argument.

Sixty seconds of sample memory, and thirty years of records that have never been mistaken for anybody else's.

# J Dilla

> Who J Dilla was and what he actually did: Conant Gardens, the sampler settings behind Dilla time, the records, Donuts, and what the sources do not support.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/j-dilla/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

In a corner house in Conant Gardens, on Detroit's east side, the family ran on shifts so the basement could keep working. Upstairs, a trained opera singer and a working jazz musician. Downstairs, their son, moving drum hits by amounts he called baby hairs.

James Dewitt Yancey, born 7 February 1974 and dead on 10 February 2006 at thirty-two, produced under the names Jay Dee and J Dilla. He is the reason a generation of drummers learned to play behind the beat on purpose. His method was to set the parts of a drum pattern against each other rather than lock them to one grid, using a sampler that let him give every track its own timing, and the result was a third way of feeling time that had not existed in American popular music before.

## The short version

- **Born**: 7 February 1974, Detroit; died 10 February 2006, Los Angeles

- **Names**: Silk, then Jay Dee, then J Dilla from around 2001

- **Machines**: SP-12, SP-1200, MPC60, MPC3000; later an SP-303 and a Minimoog Voyager

- **Groups**: Slum Village, The Ummah, Soulquarians, Jaylib

- **Records**: Fantastic Vol. 2, Welcome 2 Detroit, Ruff Draft, Champion Sound, Donuts

- **What changed**: straight time and swung time running at once, on purpose

## Conant Gardens

His mother, Maureen Yancey, known everywhere as Ma Dukes, trained as a classical and opera singer. His father, Beverly Dewitt Yancey, was a working musician, remembered by the family as a bassist. There were records in the house instead of toys from the age of two, and a family trip to the record store every Friday on payday. He took piano and cello in school. He matched pitch before he could talk.

The basement of that house was a working studio from about 1992, and the household organized itself around it. Ma Dukes's reason for tolerating the noise, in her own words: he was doing something that was good for him, he did not have to be in the streets, he was safe.

Before the sampler there were two tape decks. He made beats by pausing and recording between them, looping a whole track by hand with enough precision that Amp Fiddler, the Parliament keyboardist who lived nearby, told him he needed to separate the samples out and put them in a machine. Fiddler taught him the MPC at his own house, refused to let him read the manual, and told him to learn it by ear. Dilla said later that he never read a sampler manual again.

Fiddler also left the most useful sentence anybody has written about how he built a loop. Most people, he told Wax Poetics, would start on the one, on the kick. "He would start on the snare or the hi-hat or some other shit and just fit it into the equation, like a mathematician."

He was an MC called Silk before he was a producer called Jay Dee. He met T3 and Baatin through a rap battle in T3's grandmother's basement, and their first group was not Slum Village but Senepod. Accounts of what year Slum Village properly formed run from 1991 to 1996 and no primary source settles it.

## Q-Tip, and the years nobody could credit him

Amp Fiddler was playing keyboards for Funkadelic on the 1994 Lollapalooza tour, and when it reached Detroit he talked Q-Tip into meeting the kid with the beat tape. Busta Rhymes heard the same tape at Q-Tip's mother's house in Queens. What followed was The Ummah, a production collective that was deliberately anonymous, which is exactly why Dilla eventually walked away from it: for several years his best-known work carried a group credit rather than his name.

The Pharcyde paid him roughly $2,500 a track for Labcabincalifornia in 1995, while he was unknown. One of those tracks was "Runnin'", whose kick pattern takes twenty bars to come back round to where it started. It nearly did not survive the session. Slimkid3's account, given to The FADER in 2006: "Fat Lip and I fought physically over the way Jay Dee originally programmed 'Runnin'.' Fat Lip went in and reprogrammed every straight beat... I fought for it to be the way that it was because I was a stickler about people's creative input — that's what we hired him for." He is not being romantic about it. The people who paid for the off-grid drums were the first people to try to fix them.

By 2000 he was inside the Soulquarians circle working out of Electric Lady in New York, the loose collective around Questlove, D'Angelo, Common, Erykah Badu, Q-Tip, James Poyser and Bilal. He produced most of Common's Like Water for Chocolate and a large part of Badu's Mama's Gun. Questlove has said the collective existed partly as a delivery system for Dilla beats.

## The machines

His own account of the chain, given in what turned out to be his last interview, runs: an SP-12, then an SP-1200, then an MPC60, then its successor, then the MPC3000, and he stayed there. R.J. Rice, who signed him in 1992, gave him the SP-1200 and an Akai S950. Two machines that get attached to his name in gear roundups, an Ensoniq ASR-10 and a Casio SK-1, have no source behind them at all, and a Moog Little Phatty is chronologically impossible: it launched the month after he died.

The MPC3000 is the instrument the whole story runs through, and the reason is on one screen of its manual. The machine's internal resolution is 96 clock ticks per quarter note. Its Timing Correct page offers seven quantize values, and then three more parameters: swing percentage, shift direction and shift amount. Those three are set *per track*. Every drum voice in a pattern can be given its own swing and its own nudge, independently of every other voice.

Later there were two more instruments worth naming. A Minimoog Voyager, which he used for basslines and synth textures, now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture along with his MPC3000 Limited Edition, both donated by his mother in 2014. And a BOSS SP-303, a cheap phrase sampler with a vinyl-simulation effect, which arrived in the last year of his life. Our pieces on [the Voyager](https://gazillionindustries.com/minimoog-voyager/) and [the SP-303](https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-303/) cover both machines in detail.

## How the drums actually work

The popular version is that he turned quantize off and played by hand, and the looseness is human error left in. The scholarly version, argued at length in Charnas's Dilla Time, is that he used the quantize functions deliberately, assigning different degrees of swing to different tracks to build something that sounds machine-made and human at once. The evidence supports both at different moments, which is the honest answer: he mixed quantized, swung and hand-played tracks inside a single beat, and the mix changed from record to record. "Runnin'" is specifically documented as programmed with Timing Correct off.

The mechanism is easier to describe than the feel. MPC swing delays the off-beat subdivisions and leaves the downbeats alone; 50 percent is straight, 66.6 percent is triplet swing, and the interesting country is in between, where 60 percent gives you quintuplet swing and about 57 percent gives you septuplet swing. Set one voice at one value and another voice at a different one, and the two disagree by a fixed amount on every beat of every bar.

Charnas found the founding example by accident. A&R'ing a Chino XL record at the end of 1999, he heard hi-hats that sounded swung, loaded the track into a DAW, lined every hit up against the grid and found that the hi-hats were dead straight. It was the snare that was early, and the conflict between the two was what his ear had been reading as swing. The displacement he describes is five 192nds of a bar, which people gloss as about 65 milliseconds. On the MPC3000 that is exactly ten clock ticks, and the 65 milliseconds only holds at around 96 beats per minute, so ticks are the number to carry away, not the milliseconds.

There is no single Dilla offset, and anyone who tells you the formula is late snare and early hat has read one analysis. Measurements of different records find different configurations: straight hats with an early snare, late hats with early claps, late snares with pushing hats. What is constant is that each voice is internally consistent and the voices disagree with each other, and because it is sequenced rather than played, the same disagreement recurs identically in every bar. That is why the ear learns it as a groove instead of hearing it as a mistake.

T3, who was in the room for a decade, put the intent beyond argument in 2006: "Dilla didn't like to use a metronome or whatever, so some would be slightly off beat, but on purpose. It's just the way his ear was, crazy."

He called the moves baby hairs. He and T3 called the result simple-complex.

## What that did to drummers

Questlove's judgment is the one most often quoted, and it is a good one: the playing was as sloppy as a real musician, and so sloppy that it could not have been an accident. He has listed the words that circulated before anyone understood the intent, drunken and limping and lazy and dragging, and says he only understood it after visiting the Detroit basement. His own description of what he then went after on Voodoo is the most useful sentence in the whole literature for a producer: just the right amount off the grid.

Karriem Riggins, who played drums with him from 1996, says the feel does not map onto what a drummer would naturally do. Chris Dave worked out how to play it on a kit anyway, and is one of the main routes by which it reached modern jazz through the Robert Glasper Experiment. By 2013 NPR was calling him jazz's latest great innovator. There is now a peer-reviewed literature on how drummers learn the feel: one 2017 paper in the Journal of Popular Music Education identifies two strategies, a mathematical one that counts hi-hats in quintuplets and plays only the first and fourth of each group, and an intuitive one that relies on limb independence and a very strong internal clock to rush and drag individual voices inside one groove.

A caution that the rhythm literature earns and the harmony literature does not: there is essentially no firsthand source on his chord voicings. Every confident paragraph about Dilla's jazz harmony traces back to descriptions of what Robert Glasper plays. What is documented is the rhythm, the sampling and the mixing.

## How fast he worked

House Shoes watched him make A Tribe Called Quest's "Get a Hold" in a pre-production room at R.J. Rice's studio, roughly the size of a cubicle. The whole beat took about twelve minutes, and most of that was the drums: "He was getting frustrated on the drums... Finally got 'em and then just to chop the loop up, put it on top, took him like two, three minutes." Asked about his output generally, Shoes put it at fifteen minutes for eighty or ninety percent of the beats people know. Fifteen, twenty minutes tops.

The speed came out of the listening, not the machine. He started early and spent something like the first two hours of the day playing records end to end rather than needle-dropping for breaks, which is how a producer ends up sampling Stan Getz, Herbie Hancock, Philip Glass and Hall & Oates in the same career. What arrived at the end of those twelve minutes was usually an arrangement rather than a loop.

The chopping itself got a name after he died: micro-chopping, cutting a sample into fragments small enough that the original phrase disappears and re-sequencing them across the pads. He also pulled individual kicks and snares out of breaks, layered them and programmed a new pattern rather than letting a break run. If you want the method rather than the mythology, we have a guide to [chopping a drum break](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-chop-a-drum-break/) and one on [flipping a sample](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-flip-a-sample/).

## The mixes

Fantastic, Vol. 2 was tracked to ADATs in that Conant Gardens basement and mixed off two-inch tape through a large-format console, with samples run through a Yamaha SPX900 and kicks reinforced by a gated low-frequency oscillator around 40 Hz. That is a real studio chain doing real work, and it sits underneath a record most people file under lo-fi.

By the time he got to Los Angeles the brief had changed. His instruction to Dave Cooley, the engineer who mixed and mastered a great deal of his late work, was to make it sound like a cassette. Cooley describes the target for the shelved album that became The Diary as the washed out, gritty, mid-rangey sound Dilla wanted at that point, and says plainly that it was a flatter, thuddier mix than his earlier boom bap productions. The degradation was a decision, not a limitation.

Ruff Draft makes the point unarguable. He made it in four or five days in 2003, and his spoken introduction tells you it was recorded straight from the cassette. He made two versions, and the second added a deliberate layer of cassette distortion on top. Worth knowing if you are studying his mixing: the version most people own is the 2007 reissue, remixed from the multitracks by Cooley and Kelly Hibbert because Dilla's own mixes were thought lost. They turned up later.

Bob Power, who mixed a great deal of that era and was talking about him in 2004 while he was still alive, put his finger on why the bottom of those records works: "the kick he chooses, where he tunes it, and where the bass is in relation to that. People who mix bottom-heavy music will know that that's like 90 percent of the battle."

Mastering Donuts, Cooley timed the release of a Crane Song STC-8 to each track's tempo, on purpose, "to preserve the really disorienting compression pump, to take that intensity even a little further", and used a GML equalizer for a top end he describes as matte rather than slick. The pumping people hear on that record is not an artifact anyone tried to fix.

## The records, and the credit problem

Working out what he actually produced is harder than it should be, and the reason is The Ummah. The collective took a single group credit, so a sleeve that says "The Ummah — Producer" tells you nothing about who made which track. Two records let you get behind it.

On A Tribe Called Quest's Beats, Rhymes and Life, the printed credits carry a separate composer line, and James Yancey appears on exactly five tracks: "Get a Hold", "1nce Again", "Keeping It Moving", "Word Play" and "Stressed Out". That matches Q-Tip's own account of how many he did. On The Love Movement, the European CD prints an explicit line, Jay Dee as producer, against eight tracks. Those two sleeves are the best evidence in print, and they are worth more than any of the credit lists that circulate.

### His own records

- **Fan-Tas-Tic (Vol. 1)** (Slum Village, 1997) — assembled by Waajeed in about a week out of songs that already existed, and first sold hand to hand.

- **Fantastic, Vol. 2** (Slum Village, 2000) — tracked in the Conant Gardens basement. He left the group after it.

- **Welcome 2 Detroit** (BBE, 2001) — his solo debut album, which opened BBE's Beat Generation series.

- **Ruff Draft** (Groove Attack, 2003) — made in four or five days.

- **Champion Sound** (Jaylib, with Madlib, Stones Throw, 2003) — each producer rapping over the other's beats. Per-track production splits for this record are folklore: no printed source gives them.

- **Donuts** (Stones Throw, 2006).

- **The Shining** (BBE, 2006) — the record he was actually concentrating on, finished after his death by Karriem Riggins.

- **The Diary** (Pay Jay, 2016) — the shelved major-label album. Worth knowing: he produced four of its fourteen tracks. The rest came from Madlib, Pete Rock, Hi-Tek, Nottz, Waajeed, House Shoes, Karriem Riggins and others.

### For other people

The Pharcyde's Labcabincalifornia in 1995. Tribe, as above. Busta Rhymes, De La Soul and Janet Jackson remixes in the Ummah years. Then the run that made his reputation with people who do not buy instrumental records: Common's Like Water for Chocolate in 2000 and Electric Circus in 2002, Erykah Badu's Mama's Gun in 2000, where he also plays bass on "Booty", Bilal, Talib Kweli, Q-Tip's own records, Frank-N-Dank, Phat Kat, and Ghostface Killah's Fishscale in 2006, which used two beats that also appear on Donuts. The posthumous catalog runs from Jay Stay Paid in 2009 through Rebirth of Detroit in 2012 to The Diary in 2016, and his mother has said there are still a thousand or two unreleased pieces of music.

## Los Angeles

He moved to Los Angeles in early 2004 and lived with Common, who instigated the move and framed it as getting him out of Detroit. The major-label years had gone badly: a deal with MCA around 2001 produced an album called Pay Jay that was shelved when its champion at the label left, and Frank-N-Dank's album went the same way. He went independent instead: Ruff Draft on a German label in 2003, and Champion Sound with Madlib as Jaylib on Stones Throw the same year. The MCA record finally came out in 2016 as The Diary.

## The illness

In January 2002, just back from a European show, he collapsed. At Bon Secours Hospital in Grosse Pointe his platelet count was under 10, against a normal range of 140 to 180, and the doctors were surprised he was walking. A specialist from Harper Hospital in Detroit diagnosed thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a blood disorder, and told him there was no cure.

The lupus diagnosis that everyone now attaches to his name came later, in 2005, and the contemporaneous reporting hedged it: something that looked like lupus. Most writing since has compressed both diagnoses into 2002. It was the complications that took him apart rather than either name: recurring kidney failure, dialysis three times a week, the loss of half his body weight, the loss of the ability to walk, and repeatedly the ability to swallow.

He hid it. A magazine confirmed the hospitalization rumors in March 2004 and another downplayed the whole thing in June 2005. He signed his will on 8 September 2005. In November and December of that year he toured Europe in a wheelchair with Frank n Dank and DJ Rhettmatic, and his own group did not know about the wheelchair until they saw him in London. In Paris he was carried onto the stage through the crowd.

## Donuts

The beats began before Los Angeles. Ma Dukes has said he was working on a series of beat CDs before he came out, a project he had not named yet. What happened in the hospital room is documented in detail by the Detroit Free Press reporter who was with the family in 2006: the tools of his trade surrounded him, turntables, headphones, crates of records, a sampler, his drum machine and a computer, carried in by his mother and by friends from Stones Throw. Karriem Riggins remembers a small BOSS SP-303 and a portable 45 player. The Free Press reported that before September 2005 ended he had completed all but two songs. When his hands swelled shut, his mother massaged his fingers so he could keep going.

He would not let anyone hear it. Ma Dukes has described sneaking in to listen while he was in dialysis, and how angry he was when he found out.

The album as you own it is also an editorial act. Stones Throw's art director Jeff Jank worked with him on the edit and the sequence, expanding a beat tape of about 27 tracks into the thirty-one-track record, with nine late additions among them; the work of assembly, in Jank's words, happened entirely while Dilla was at Cedars-Sinai. Asked to extend the tape himself, Dilla reportedly told them to do it. He was concentrating on The Shining. The last seconds of Donuts are the same as its first, so on repeat it never stops.

It came out on 7 February 2006, his thirty-second birthday, and the first birthday in four years he had not spent in a hospital. He had relearned how to swallow and traded the wheelchair for a walker weeks earlier. He died three days later, on 10 February, at home in Los Angeles. The cause given at the time was cardiac arrest, stated by his mother, after a recent hospitalization for pneumonia. No autopsy has ever been reported. There was a public viewing at Forest Lawn on 13 February and a private funeral on the 14th, and a memorial in Detroit later that month that more than three hundred people came to.

Pitchfork gave Donuts a 7.9 the day after it was released. When the same publication reviewed the reissue in 2013 it gave it a 10.

## What the record does not support

More gets repeated about Dilla than about almost any producer, and a fair amount of it does not survive contact with the sources. These are the ones worth knowing, because each is load-bearing for somebody's argument.

- **"He never quantized."** The biographer who spent four years and nearly two hundred interviews on him is blunt about this: it is not true. He used the machine's timing functions, per track, deliberately. Some tracks were quantized, some were swung by different amounts, some were played free.

- **"He made Donuts in his hospital bed."** He worked in the hospital, on equipment carried in by his mother and Stones Throw, and that much is attested by everyone involved. But a beat tape of the material existed before the final hospitalization, and the album as released was expanded, edited and sequenced by Jeff Jank. Both halves of that are true, and the second half does not diminish the first.

- **"The track titles are his goodbye letter."** Jank named the tracks.

- **"He produced Janet Jackson's 'Got 'Til It's Gone' and Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis took the credit."** Dilla himself told a version of this in a 2003 interview. Q-Tip was asked about it directly in 2009 and gave a different account: Janet's camp heard beats he and Dilla had made, and it inspired them to make their own record, which is why it sounded familiar. There are real Ummah remixes of the track, which is where some of the confusion lives.

- **"He played everything on Welcome 2 Detroit."** He produced all but one track and played on several. Karriem Riggins played drums and produced "The Clapper"; Dwele played keys, bass and trumpet on "Think Twice", with his brother Antwan Gardener on trombone.

- **"Bob Moog built him a custom Voyager and signed the faceplate."** The Smithsonian's press release calls the instrument custom-made, and the story has grown from there. The museum's own catalog record notes no signature, and the serial number sits inside the 600-unit first run that shipped to everybody.

- **"He died of lupus, at Cedars-Sinai."** He died at home in Los Angeles. The blood disorder diagnosed in 2002 was TTP; the lupus label came later and the reporting closest to the family hedged it at the time.

- **"He produced 'Devil's Pie' on Voodoo."** D'Angelo's Voodoo carries no Dilla production credit at all. He was part of the Soulquarians circle that made the record; that is a different claim.

- **The gear lists.** An Ensoniq ASR-10 and a Casio SK-1 turn up in almost every roundup of his equipment with nothing behind them, and his own account of his machines does not include either. A Moog Little Phatty is impossible: it launched the month after he died.

## The person, as opposed to the saint

Almost every published portrait of him says shy, quiet, humble. That is true and it is incomplete, and the people closest to him are the ones who said so. His mother, in the 33 1/3 book on Donuts: "He got stronger, I guess from the knocks of coming along in [the music industry], and he became just outright belligerent at times. He never backed down... we would get neck and neck sometimes." House Shoes, in the same book, is blunter about what it was like to be on the wrong side of him.

The same book documents him falling out with his own label over a bootleg, with a friend over revealing he was in hospital, and with House Shoes over a crate of records, a fight that ended up as a diss on a Jaylib record. He was twenty-seven when he was told there was no cure. The canonization started immediately after he died and has not really stopped, and it is worth remembering that the person it happened to was not a monument.

Drums that came off a record, squashed on the way out. **DOSE 88**, and the line along the bottom is the gain reduction recovering across the bar.

## The afterlife

On 17 July 2014, at the annual DC Loves Dilla concert, his mother announced that she was giving his equipment to the Smithsonian. The National Museum of African American History and Culture accessioned the MPC3000 Limited Edition, its gold plaque reading edition number 0449, and the Minimoog Voyager, serial 263, along with the power cord, a cable and the factory case. Both are in the museum's Musical Crossroads exhibition. She had refused at first. The curator, Timothy Anne Burnside, spent years talking her round.

That is an unusual destination for a drum machine, and it is the clearest institutional statement of what he is understood to have done: the objects are there as instruments of American music history, in the same building as the rest of it.

The estate took longer and went worse. He signed a will in September 2005 naming his mother, his two daughters and his brother, with an accountant as executor. In 2008 an unfinished album leaked and the family's objections played out in public, including a full-page advertisement in Billboard. The executor resigned in 2009 after the family challenged the administration, and control passed through another administrator before his mother and his brother Illa J finally held it themselves. She has spent two decades doing that work in public, and has said she spent years unable to draw anything from his catalog at all.

The critical apparatus arrived late but solidly. Dan Charnas's biography, published in 2022, reframed him as a rhythmic innovator rather than a cult producer, was reviewed everywhere from the New York Times to the LA Times, and won a PEN award the following year. Charnas teaches a course on him at New York University. There have been museum exhibitions at Wayne State, The Broad and Guild Hall. In 2024 Detroit's city council passed a resolution honoring him, sponsored by its president, and the city named a street after him near the house he grew up in.

the drum programming behind it is a set of things you can actually do, collected in [how to make Dilla type beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-dilla-type-beats/)

## Questions people ask

### What was the cause of J Dilla's death?

He died at home in Los Angeles on 10 February 2006, at thirty-two, three days after Donuts was released on his birthday. The cause given at the time was cardiac arrest, stated by his mother, after years of complications and a recent hospitalization for pneumonia. No autopsy has ever been reported.

### What illness did J Dilla have?

In January 2002 he collapsed and was found to have a platelet count under 10, against a normal range of 140 to 180. A specialist diagnosed thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a rare blood disorder, and told him there was no cure. A lupus diagnosis came later, in 2005, and the reporting closest to the family hedged it even then. The complications, not the labels, are what disabled him: kidney failure, dialysis three times a week, and the loss of half his body weight.

### Why is J Dilla considered so important?

Because he built a third way of feeling time and then proved it on records other people paid for. Before him, American popular music had straight time and swung time. He ran both at once, by giving each voice in a drum pattern its own timing, and the result was strange enough that musicians spent the next twenty years learning to play it on acoustic instruments.

### What is special about Dilla's drums?

Each voice sits in a consistent place that is not the grid, and the voices disagree with each other. Because it is sequenced rather than played, the same disagreement repeats identically in every bar, so the ear learns it as a groove instead of hearing it as a mistake. There is no single offset: measurements of different records find early snares, late hats, straight hats and dragging claps, depending on the record.

### How do you make beats like J Dilla?

Give the parts different timing instead of nudging the whole pattern. Set the hats to one swing value and the snare to another, or quantize one voice and play another by hand, then leave it alone so the displacement repeats. Choose samples that were played loosely to begin with. And start the loop somewhere other than the kick. Our guides to [boom bap drums](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-boom-bap-drums/) and [chopping a drum break](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-chop-a-drum-break/) cover the mechanics.

### What equipment did J Dilla use?

By his own account: an SP-12, then an SP-1200, then an MPC60 and its successor, then the MPC3000, which he stayed on. He also had an Akai S950 early, a Minimoog Voyager from 2002, and a BOSS SP-303 in his last year. The MPC3000 Limited Edition and the Voyager are both in the Smithsonian.

### What was J Dilla's real name?

James Dewitt Yancey. He recorded as Jay Dee for most of his career and changed it to J Dilla around 2001, to stop being confused with the producer Jermaine Dupri.

The house in Conant Gardens ran on shifts so the basement could keep working. Twenty-odd years after it stopped, drummers in conservatories are being taught to play what came out of it.

# Kenny Segal

> How Kenny Segal makes records: live players over samples, the SP-404 used as an effects box, drums edited hit by hit, and sampling the spaces between the notes.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/kenny-segal/  
Published 2026-09-20, updated 2026-09-24. By Gazillion Industries.

---

Most producers who get called an SP-404 user are describing a sampler. In this case the machine is closer to a pedalboard: live drums, played in a room, running out through a cheap box of effects and back in again, until the recording stops sounding like a recording.

Kenny Segal is a Los Angeles producer best known for his records with billy woods — Hiding Places in 2019 and Maps in 2023 — and for work with R.A.P. Ferreira, Armand Hammer, Open Mike Eagle and Busdriver. His method is built around live musicians playing over samples, and the SP-404 sits in that chain as a processor rather than as the thing the beat is made on. His own description: start with the sample, get a vibe, then have people come and play on top of it.

## The short version

- **Known for**: Hiding Places (2019), Maps (2023) with billy woods

- **Studio**: a home room in Jefferson Park, Los Angeles

- **Samplers**: reported as a cache of SP-404s

- **Plays**: Omnichord and a Bastl MicroGranny on record

- **Method**: sample first, then live players over it

- **Signature**: sampling the spaces between the notes

## The 404 as an effects unit

The clearest public document of how he uses the machine is a sample pack he put out in 2017, because one of its folders is labeled for exactly what it contains: live drums processed through SP-404 effects. Not drums sequenced on a 404. Drums played, recorded, and then run through the box for what it does to them.

The same pack includes a circuit-bent Omnichord, a hacked toy sampler, and a folder of vinyl noise, tape hiss and field recordings. That is a fair picture of the palette: acoustic sources and broken electronics, with a cheap sampler's effects as the glue. If you want to know what the 404's ancestors did to audio in that role, our piece on [the SP-303](https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-303/) covers it, and [the SP-404 story](https://gazillionindustries.com/sp-404-history/) covers how the line got there.

## Sampling the spaces between the notes

That phrase is his, and it is the most useful idea in his published method. Ableton put out a breakdown of his approach in 2017 with a downloadable session, and the structure is revealing: each drum element sits on its own arrangement track rather than in a clip, so that any individual hit can be muted, reversed or pitched on its own.

What that gives you is not a loop with variations. It is a performance you can edit at the level of the single hit, which is why his drums breathe in a way programmed drums usually do not and why they never quite repeat. The spaces are the material: the bar of room tone between two phrases, the breath before a horn line, the decay nobody else kept.

[Gazillion Industries](https://gazillionindustries.com/) makes plugins for records built this way, where the room and the noise are the content rather than the problem.

## The room, from the people in it

Musicians who have recorded there describe a Rhodes, a Casio CZ-101, a polyphonic Moog, a spread of pedals, and a microphone and preamp collection good enough that one of them singled out how clear the drums came back. They also describe him working the controls during takes rather than afterward, which fits everything else about the method: the processing is part of the performance, not a stage that happens later.

Small practical detail worth stealing: on at least one record the guitars went straight in, with no amplifier. A guitar direct into a chain of samplers and pedals is a different instrument from a guitar in front of a speaker, and on the right record it is the better one.

## Why the records sound like that

Hiding Places and Maps are rap records where the instrumental rarely behaves like a beat. The loops drift, the drums arrive late or not at all, and there are long passages where what is holding time is a musician rather than a grid. That is a direct consequence of the working order: if the sample comes first and the players come second, what you end up with is a performance of a loop rather than a loop with performances on top.

It is also the opposite of the dominant approach, where the grid is fixed first and everything is fitted to it. Both produce good records. They produce different kinds.

## Questions people ask

### What does Kenny Segal use?

A home studio in Los Angeles with a reported cache of SP-404s, a Rhodes, a Casio CZ-101, a polyphonic Moog, pedals, and a good microphone and preamp collection. He plays Omnichord and a Bastl MicroGranny on record.

### How does he use the SP-404?

Mostly as an effects processor on material played live, rather than as the sequencer. His own sample pack documents live drums run through the machine's effects.

### What is his production process?

In his words: start with the sample, get a vibe, then bring musicians in to play over it. The drums are then edited at the level of individual hits, each on its own track.

### What records should I start with?

Hiding Places with billy woods (2019) and Maps (2023). Then the work with R.A.P. Ferreira, Armand Hammer and Open Mike Eagle.

The drum bus end of it, in one control.

We make [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html). The drum bus end of it, in one control.

## What to take from it

Two things. Put the processor in the performance rather than after it: if a cheap sampler's effects are going to be on the drums, run the drums through them while people are playing and commit. And treat every hit as editable rather than every bar: a kit on separate tracks, where one snare can be reversed or dropped, is a different instrument from a loop.

The machine everyone associates with him was never really the point. The players in the room were.
