# Best lead synth VST: how to choose a synth lead plugin

> What makes the best lead synth VST: one voice, glide, filter slope and modulation you can reach, plus the paid and free synth lead plugins people name.

Source: https://gazillionindustries.com/best-lead-synth-vst/  
Published 2026-09-26, updated 2026-09-26. By Gazillion Industries, who make JOURNEYMAN.

---

The beat is finished and the lead is the problem. It plays the right notes in the right register, and in the car it still sounds like a keyboard demo somebody left running underneath the drums — present, in tune, carrying none of the tune.

For a single melodic line, the best lead synth VST is a monosynth: one voice, so each note hands over to the next instead of stacking on top of it, with glide, note priority and a filter you can play with your hands. [JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html) is ours, $59, and it is the plug-in worked through below. After that, the mechanism, a build from scratch, and the other synths people name.

## The short version

- **The job**: one line, one note at a time, loud enough to carry the melody

- **Why mono**: glide, note priority and single trigger only exist when there is one voice

- **What decides it**: filter slope and resonance, a fast attack, modulation under your hands

- **What to use**: [JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html), $59 — three oscillators, two ladder filters, glide, 200 programs

- **Free route**: Vital's Basic tier, Surge XT, and the synth already in your DAW

- **Worst habit**: building the lead as a chord, then fighting it for the rest of the mix

**One voice, laid out in the order you build it.** Oscillators and mixer top left, filters and envelopes right, everything that moves on its own along the bottom.

## What a lead actually has to do

A lead carries the melody over everything else in the arrangement. That is one sentence with three demands buried in it: it has to be heard through a dense mix, it has to be recognizable after four bars, and it has to sound like one instrument rather than a stack of them. Most synth leads fail the third test before they get near the first two.

The register is where the trouble starts. A lead usually lives between roughly 500 Hz and 4 kHz, which is also where the ear is at its most sensitive and where the vocal, the snare and the top of the sample all want to be. You are not competing with the low end. You are competing with everything that survives a phone speaker, and that fight is covered in [Fletcher-Munson](https://gazillionindustries.com/fletcher-munson/).

A lead also has to move. A held note with a fixed timbre stops being information about eight seconds in. Something has to change while the note sounds, or the listener files the part as furniture and goes back to the drums.

## Why the best lead synth VST is usually a monosynth

A monosynth plays one note at a time. That reads like a limitation on a spec sheet and it is the reason the category exists. When an instrument can only hold one note, the engineering goes into what happens between notes rather than into how many can sound at once, and between notes is exactly where a lead lives.

### One voice means the notes connect

Play a fast run on a polysynth with any release at all and the tails overlap. Six notes into a sixteenth-note line you have four voices sounding, the filter envelope has retriggered four times, and the sum is a smear with the rhythm buried in it. A single voice cannot do that. Each new note takes the voice over, and the line stays a line.

You can hear it on a laptop speaker. Bounce the same MIDI through both and the mono version reads as a melody while the poly version reads as a texture. Neither is wrong. Only one of them is a lead.

### Note priority and trigger, the two settings nobody reads

When two notes overlap on a one-voice instrument, something has to decide which one wins. **Last** priority gives the voice to the most recent key, which is what you want for a played line. **Low** and **high** priority hand it to the bottom or top note instead, which is how you play a moving line against a pedal tone with one hand.

Trigger mode is the companion setting. On **multi** trigger every new note fires both envelopes again, so each note has its own attack. On **single** trigger an overlapping note takes the pitch without restarting the envelopes, so a legato phrase opens once and stays open. Those two switches change the feel of a part more than any preset will.

### Glide is a lead instrument's accent

Glide slides the pitch from the note you left to the note you arrived at, over a time you set. Around 20 to 60 ms it reads as an accent on the front of the note. At 200 ms and up it reads as a slide and starts eating the rhythm. Paired with single trigger it only runs when notes overlap, so you play the slides in rather than program them: hold the last note a sixteenth longer than you should and the next one arrives bent.

[JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html) is our monosynth for Mac and Windows: one voice, three oscillators, two ladder filters spread left and right, two envelopes, two modulation busses and 200 programs across basses, leads, keys, pads, percussion and fx. There's a demo on the page.

## What separates the best synth lead plugins from the loudest ones

Most of the difference between synth lead plugins comes down to seven things, none of which appear in the marketing, and each one can be checked in your own session in a minute.

### Detune between oscillators, and how slow it beats

Two oscillators at slightly different pitches beat at the difference frequency. Tune them 1 Hz apart and the amplitude swells once a second; 5 Hz apart and it flutters. For a lead the slow end is the one that sounds like an instrument, because the swell happens over a note rather than inside it. What varies between synths is resolution: sweep the fine tuning slowly on a held note and listen for jumps. The same principle applied to whole tracks is in [detune plugins](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-detune-plugins/).

### Filter slope, stated in poles

A low-pass filter's steepness is measured in poles, and each pole sheds 6 dB per octave above the corner. Four poles roll off at 24 dB per octave and close down to something dark and hollow; three poles roll off at 18 dB per octave and leave more of the top audible at the same cutoff setting. For a lead that has to be heard, the shallower option often survives the mix better. Being able to choose matters more than which one a synth ships with — the mechanism is in [filter cutoff and resonance](https://gazillionindustries.com/filter-cutoff-and-resonance/).

### Resonance that stays playable

Resonance lifts a peak at the corner frequency. A little makes a filter sweep sing; too much turns the synth into a sine wave at the cutoff and takes the body with it. Park the cutoff around 800 Hz, raise resonance to the top, and play a two-octave run. If the loudness swings wildly as notes pass under the peak, you will be fighting that on every part you write.

### Two filters, and what they do to your stereo image

Running a voice through two filters at different cutoffs, one panned left and one right, makes a mono source sound wide. It is a real width with a real cost: the two sides no longer contain the same signal, so summing to mono changes the tone. Check it before you commit — the mechanism is in [phase cancellation](https://gazillionindustries.com/phase-cancellation/) and the test is in [mono compatibility](https://gazillionindustries.com/mono-compatibility/).

### An envelope with a genuinely fast attack

The front of a note is where a lead announces itself. If the fastest attack setting still takes 10 ms to reach full level, every note starts soft and the part sits behind the drums however loud you make it. Record the synth to an audio track, zoom in on one note, and look at the first rise. The waveform tells you in a second what a spec sheet will not.

### Oscillator sync and cross-modulation

Hard sync restarts one oscillator every time another completes a cycle. You get a fixed pitch with a timbre that changes as the synced oscillator is swept, which is the hard, vocal, tearing lead you already recognize. Frequency modulation between two audio-rate oscillators gives the other family: bells and metal at low amounts, chaos above that. Both throw harmonics far above the fundamental, so sweep a synced lead up two octaves and listen for tones moving the wrong way. That is [aliasing](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-aliasing-in-audio/), and once you hear it you cannot unhear it.

### Modulation you can reach while playing

A matrix with forty slots is a sound design tool. A mod wheel wired to one destination with an amount you set is a performance tool, and a lead is performed. The question to ask of any synth lead VST is not how many routings it has but how many of them your hands can get to without stopping the transport.

## Build a lead from scratch

Building one from a single oscillator takes about ten minutes and is the fastest way to learn where an instrument hides its character. The steps are written for JOURNEYMAN's panel; the order works on any monosynth.

- Press INIT to clear the panel to a starting state.

- Set OSC 1 OCTAVE to 8' and turn WAVE to the sawtooth position.

- Raise OSC 1 in the MIXER until the level reads healthy and the OVERLOAD lamp stays dark.

- Play the melody in and move OCTAVE until the line sits above the bass and below the hats.

- Switch OSC 2 on, set its OCTAVE to 8', and turn FREQUENCY until you hear one beat per second.

- Set OSC 3 OCTAVE to 16' and bring it up under the other two until the line has weight.

- Close CUTOFF until the top stops hissing, then raise RESONANCE until the corner sings and back it off one mark.

- Set FILTER ENV ATTACK to 0, DECAY to about 3, SUSTAIN to about 5, then raise AMOUNT until each note opens.

- Set VOLUME ENV ATTACK to 0 and RELEASE short enough that the notes stop when you do.

- Turn GLIDE on and set GLIDE RATE so a jump of a fifth arrives in roughly 40 ms.

- Set TRIGGER to SINGLE so the glide only runs between overlapping notes.

- Set the MOD WHEEL BUS DESTINATION to OSC 2 with a low AMOUNT, then ride the wheel on held notes.

- Bounce eight bars and play them on your phone before you save the program.

## Where the synth lead sits in the mix

A lead that needs volume to be heard is usually a lead with the wrong spectrum. Before you reach for the fader, find the two or three narrow bands where the part actually speaks and check that nothing else is sitting in them. On most records the lead and the vocal are fighting over the same 2 to 4 kHz, and one of them has to give it up.

Saturation is the cheaper fix. Harmonics above the fundamental give a part presence on small speakers without adding level, which matters because most phone speakers give you almost nothing below a few hundred hertz. Mechanism in [harmonic distortion](https://gazillionindustries.com/harmonic-distortion/), practice in [how to make a synth sound thicker](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-a-synth-sound-thicker/), small speakers in [bass on phone speakers](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-bass-audible-on-phone-speakers/).

Compression on a lead is about evenness rather than loudness. We give away a one-knob compressor for that job: [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html) is free for Mac and Windows, and the wider list is in [best free compressor](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-free-compressor/). Set your levels first either way — a synth clipping inside the plug-in sounds like a synth with a bad filter, and the fix is three dB lower rather than a different instrument. See [gain staging](https://gazillionindustries.com/gain-staging/).

## Free synth lead VST options worth the download

There are good free ones. None are monosynths, so the note handoff above still applies, but if the budget is zero today, start here.

### Vital

Vital's Basic tier is free on the developer's own site and includes the full synth with all features, 75 presets and 25 wavetables; the paid tiers add presets and wavetables rather than capability. For anybody learning what modulation does, the animated display alone is worth the download.

### The synth already in your DAW

Every major DAW ships a subtractive synth with oscillators, a filter and two envelopes, and most of them have a mono or legato switch buried in the voice settings. Find that switch before you download anything. It will tell you whether the problem with your lead was the instrument or the arrangement.

## What a monosynth costs you

One voice means no chords. If your part has two notes sounding at once anywhere, a monosynth plays one and drops the other, and you find out during the bounce rather than during the take. The workaround is a second instance on a second track, which costs you the shared glide and shared filter movement that made you want one voice to begin with.

A single voice also exposes your playing: no second note to hide behind, no tail from the previous chord smoothing over a late attack. That is a cost, and it is also why the good leads on records sound played rather than drawn.

## Four mistakes worth not making

**Writing the lead last.** A melody written over a finished arrangement inherits every hole that arrangement left, which is usually the wrong register. Write the line early, even if you replace the sound later.

**Solving a dull lead with more detune.** Detune widens. It does not make a part more interesting, and past a certain amount it makes the pitch ambiguous, which on a melody is fatal. If the line is boring, the line is boring.

**Automating the filter instead of playing it.** A drawn curve has the rhythm of a mouse. Assign cutoff to the mod wheel or the touch surface, record a pass, keep the take — the long version is in [how to make a filter sweep](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-a-filter-sweep/).

**Judging the sound in solo.** A lead that sounds thin alone is often perfect in the mix, and one that sounds huge alone is usually eating the vocal. Solo finds problems. It does not make decisions.

### Why does my synth lead disappear in the mix?

Usually one of three things. The attack is too slow, so every note starts underneath the drums instead of on top of them. # Best monosynth VST

Published 2026-09-26, updated 2026-09-26. By Gazillion Industries, who make JOURNEYMAN.

---

The bass line owns the room on monitors and disappears in the car. Four saw layers, detuned, a chorus over the top, and somewhere in the stacking the note stopped being a note. You can hear the arrangement working; you cannot hear the pitch.

The best monosynth VST is the one you can play: glide that tracks the interval, envelopes fast enough to put an attack on the front of a note, and a filter that stays musical with resonance up. One voice at a time is the point, because everything the instrument has goes into that voice. [JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html) is $59, carries all three, and is the synth worked through below. Then the architecture, a ten-minute test, six patches, and the other plug-ins people name.

## The short version

- **What a monosynth is**: a synthesizer that sounds one note at a time

- **Why one voice**: glide, note priority and the whole engine spent on a single line

- **What decides quality**: envelope speed, resonance that stays playable, glide that tracks

- **What to use**: [JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html), $59 — three oscillators, two ladder filters, 200 programs

- **Free route**: Surge XT or Odin 2, both free, both polyphonic synths you hold to one voice

- **What it costs**: no chords, and one slow envelope setting flattens the groove

**One voice, laid out left to right.** Oscillators into the mixer, the mixer into two filters, the filters into an amplifier the volume envelope opens and closes.

## What a monosynth plugin actually is

A monosynth sounds one note at a time. Play a second key while the first is held and the instrument does not start a second voice; it moves the voice it already has to the new pitch. That single rule is what separates the instrument from a polysynth set to one voice, and it is what every technique below is built on.

The consequence is that a monosynth cannot play a chord. Stack three notes in the piano roll and you will hear one of them, chosen by whatever priority rule the synth uses. If you want the chord, you run three instances or you write it on something polyphonic. A monosynth plugin is for the line: bass, lead, counter-melody, a riser, a bleep on the offbeat.

What you get back for that restriction is control. Every oscillator, every filter and every modulation source is pointed at a single note, so a small move is audible immediately, and the gestures that only make sense on one voice — glide between two pitches, a filter sweep that belongs to the phrase rather than to a chord — become the instrument's whole personality.

### Glide, and why it only exists here

Glide is the time the pitch takes to travel from the old note to the new one. Set it to 0 ms and notes step. Set it to 120 ms and a fifth slides. On a polysynth the idea barely works, because there is no single "old note" to travel from when four voices are ringing. On one voice the origin is never in doubt.

Glide time is either constant time or constant rate. Constant time means every interval takes the same number of milliseconds, so an octave and a semitone both take 120 ms and the octave sounds faster. Constant rate means the pitch travels at a fixed speed, so the octave takes twelve times as long as the semitone. Bass lines usually want the second; a lead usually wants the first.

### Note priority and trigger modes

Note priority decides which held key wins. Low-note priority keeps the bottom of whatever you are holding, which is the usual choice for bass. High-note priority keeps the top, which suits a lead where you want trills to read. Last-note priority follows your fingers exactly and is the most literal of the three.

Trigger mode decides whether the envelopes restart. Single trigger, sometimes called legato, leaves the envelope running when you play a new note while the old one is held, so an overlapping phrase keeps one continuous shape. Multi trigger restarts the envelope on every note, so each note gets its own attack. Overlap two sixteenths at 120 BPM, which is 125 ms each, and the difference between the two modes is the whole feel of the line.

## The parts of a monosynth, in signal order

Almost every monosynth, in hardware or in a plug-in, runs the same chain. Oscillators make raw waveforms, a mixer sets their balance, a filter removes what you do not want, an amplifier shaped by an envelope decides when you hear it, and a set of modulators move the rest while you play. Know the chain and every panel you meet becomes readable.

### Oscillators

An oscillator produces a repeating waveform at a pitch. A triangle is nearly a sine with a little edge. A sawtooth carries every harmonic and is the default for anything that needs to sound big. A square carries odd harmonics only and sounds hollow, woody, faintly clarinet. Narrow the square into a pulse and it thins out and starts to buzz.

Two or three oscillators together is where the size comes from. Tune one an octave down for weight, or detune two by a few cents against each other for movement. The arithmetic is worth knowing: two oscillators three cents apart at 110 Hz differ by 0.19 Hz, which is one slow swell every 5.2 seconds. Ten cents apart at 55 Hz is 0.32 Hz, a swell every 3.1 seconds, and on a sustained bass note that is already too much movement. Our piece on [detune](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-detune-plugins/) works through what those beat rates do in a mix.

Two other oscillator tricks show up constantly on monosynths. Hard sync locks one oscillator's cycle to another's, so sweeping the synced oscillator's pitch produces that tearing, vowel-like sweep instead of a pitch change. Frequency modulation at audio rate uses one oscillator to modulate another's pitch, which gives you bell tones, clangs and metal.

### The mixer, noise and external input

The mixer sets how much of each oscillator reaches the filter, and it is the most underrated control on any monosynth plugin. Balance decides whether a patch is a sub with a little edge or an edge with a little sub. A noise source in the same mixer gives you breath, wind and the front of a snare. An external input lets you send a drum loop or a vocal through the synth's filter and amplifier instead of an oscillator.

### Filters

A low-pass filter keeps what is below a corner frequency and sheds what is above it. The rate of that fall is set by the pole count: each pole is 6 dB per octave, so a 3-pole filter sheds 18 dB every time the frequency doubles and a 4-pole sheds 24 dB. With the corner at 500 Hz, a 4-pole is 24 dB down at 1 kHz and 48 dB down at 2 kHz.

Resonance is a boost at the corner itself, and it is where cheap filters give themselves away. A narrow peak at the corner is what makes a sweep sound like a sweep rather than a slow fade, and pushed far enough it dominates everything else in the patch. Our longer piece on [cutoff and resonance](https://gazillionindustries.com/filter-cutoff-and-resonance/) covers the tradeoff in detail.

Two filters instead of one changes the instrument. Run them at different corner frequencies and the gap between them becomes a tone control of its own. Run them on the left and right sides and that gap becomes width: the same note, filtered two ways, one per speaker. Check the result in [mono](https://gazillionindustries.com/mono-compatibility/) before you commit, because width made by difference is width that can partly disappear when a club system sums the sides.

### Envelopes

An envelope is a shape in time with four numbers. Attack is how long the level takes to reach the top, decay how long it takes to fall to the sustain level, sustain the level it holds at while the key is down, release how long it takes to fall to silence after you let go. Two envelopes is the standard: one for volume, one for the filter.

Attack time is the number that decides whether a patch sounds like an instrument or like a pad someone forgot to shorten. Under about 5 ms a note has a front edge you feel; at 50 ms it swells; at 500 ms it is a fade-in and the groove has gone. The same applies to the filter envelope, where a fast attack and a short decay gives you the pluck at the start of a note. Our piece on [transients](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-a-transient/) is the background.

### LFO and modulation busses

An LFO is an oscillator running below hearing, from a fraction of a hertz up to around 20 Hz, whose output moves a control rather than making a sound. Aimed at pitch it is vibrato. Aimed at the filter it is a wobble. Aimed at pulse width it thickens a square. A sample-and-hold setting picks a new random value on every tick and stays there, which is the sound of every bubbling sequence ever written.

A modulation bus is a small routing strip: pick a source, pick a destination, set an amount, and decide what controls the amount. Two busses on one voice is plenty, and having them wired to the mod wheel and a pedal is what turns a static patch into something you perform. The amount knob matters more than the source. A vibrato at full depth is seasickness; the same vibrato at eight percent is a singer.

[JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html) is our monosynth: one voice, three oscillators, two ladder filters with a SPACING control between them, two ADSR envelopes, an LFO with sample and hold, and 200 programs across basses, leads, keys, pads, percussion and fx. There's a demo on the page.

## What separates a good monosynth plugin from a bad one

Eight things, and only two of them appear on a feature list. This is the checklist we use when a synth arrives, and it is the same one worth running before you spend anything.

### Envelope speed at the fast end

Set attack and decay to their minimum, sustain to zero, and play a low note. A good envelope gives you a click you can use as a percussion hit. A slow one gives you a soft blip no matter what the numbers say. This single test tells you whether the synth can do plucks, keys and drum sounds, or only pads.

### Resonance that stays playable

Take resonance to three quarters and sweep the cutoff across the full range. Listen for the peak swamping the rest of the patch, for the level jumping as the peak crosses a strong harmonic, and for the low end thinning out as resonance rises. A filter you can only use below half resonance is half a filter.

### Glide that tracks the interval

Play a semitone and then an octave with the same glide setting. If both take the same time, you have constant time. If the octave takes twelve times as long, you have constant rate. Either is fine; not knowing which one you have is what makes a bass line land in the wrong place.

### Tuning you can set precisely

Detune between oscillators has to be settable in cents, not by feel on an unmarked knob. The difference between 3 cents and 12 cents on a sustained bass note is the difference between a patch that sits still and a patch that wobbles through the bar.

### A second filter, or a reason not to have one

Two filters with a spacing control give you width, a nasal mid-band, or a band-pass you can play. If a synth has only one, check that it at least offers high-pass as well as low-pass, so you can clear room under a lead without reaching for an EQ.

### Modulation you can reach while playing

The mod wheel and a pedal input are the only two modulators you can operate with your hands busy. A synth where every program is already wired to the wheel is a synth you will perform; one where you have to build the routing first is a synth you will program once and then leave alone.

### Programs that are starting points

A good factory bank teaches the panel. Load a bass, look at where the oscillators are tuned, see how far the filter envelope is opening the cutoff, and you have learned something you can reuse. Sold-as-magic preset packs teach nothing, which is why the count matters far less than whether the programs are readable.

### Formats, CPU and the boring part

Check the formats before anything else. AU matters on Mac, VST3 matters everywhere, and a standalone build matters if you ever want to play without opening a DAW. Then load eight instances and watch the meter, because a monosynth is a plug-in you will end up running several of.

## How to test a mono synth plugin in ten minutes

Do this before you buy anything, in your own session, on your own speakers. Ten minutes gets you further than an hour of reading roundups, this one included.

- Load the synth on a fresh track and open the simplest bass program in the bank.

- Set attack to 0 ms, decay to 0 ms and sustain to maximum, so you hear the raw voice.

- Play A1 at 55 Hz and hold it for four bars.

- Sweep the filter cutoff from fully closed to fully open and back, once, slowly.

- Raise resonance to 75 percent and repeat the sweep.

- Set sustain to 0 and decay to 80 ms, then play sixteenths at 120 BPM.

- Set glide to 120 ms and play a semitone, then an octave, and time both.

- Detune the second oscillator by 3 cents, then by 12 cents, holding a note through each.

- Switch between single and multi trigger while playing an overlapping phrase.

- Bounce eight bars and play it back on a phone speaker and in the car.

Step ten is the one people skip. A phone speaker gives you almost nothing under 500 Hz, so a bass patch that reads as enormous on monitors can vanish entirely, and the fix is upper harmonics rather than more sub. Our guide on [bass on phone speakers](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-bass-audible-on-phone-speakers/) works through the arithmetic.

## Six patches worth building by hand

Every one of these starts from an initialized voice rather than a program, because building them is how the panel stops being a picture. The control names below are JOURNEYMAN's; the shapes transfer to any monosynth plugin with the same parts.

### Sub bass that survives the car

One oscillator, triangle, an octave down. Second oscillator at the same pitch on a saw, mixed about 20 dB under the first, purely for the harmonics a small speaker can reproduce. Cutoff around 400 Hz, resonance at zero, volume envelope with a 2 ms attack and full sustain. The saw is doing the work on the phone even though you can barely hear it on monitors.

### Rubber funk bass

Two oscillators, square and saw, three cents apart. Filter envelope with a 0 ms attack, a 90 ms decay and zero sustain, opening the cutoff by roughly an octave and a half. Glide at 60 ms, low-note priority, single trigger, and then write the line with a few overlaps so the glide has somewhere to go. The pluck comes from the decay, and the slide comes from the overlaps.

### Lead that cuts a dense beat

Three oscillators: one at pitch, one an octave up, one a fifth up, all saws. Cutoff high, resonance around 30 percent, filter envelope shallow. Then open the spacing between the two filters so the second sits well above the first, which gives the lead a fixed nasal band that survives everything else in the arrangement. If it still hides behind the drums, the next move is [thickening the synth](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-a-synth-sound-thicker/) rather than turning it up.

### Keys under a dusty loop

Square wave on its own, filter around 1.2 kHz, no resonance. Volume envelope with a 4 ms attack, a 600 ms decay, sustain at about 30 percent, release around 250 ms. Play it with two fingers and let the glide off entirely. This is the sound that sits under a [loop with a real drummer's timing](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-dilla-type-beats/) without fighting it.

### Percussion from one oscillator

Noise only in the mixer, both envelopes at zero attack, zero sustain, decay around 40 ms. Cutoff high for a hat, mid with resonance up for a rimshot. Then swap the noise for a triangle at a low pitch, put the filter envelope's decay at 25 ms and the pitch modulation at a large amount, and you have a kick. Layer it under the ones you already have and see [what it adds](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-drums-hit-harder/).

### An FX sweep with an end

Noise plus a detuned saw, cutoff low, resonance at 80 percent, LFO on the cutoff at a bar-long rate. Set the volume envelope release to 1.5 seconds so the sweep has a tail rather than a cut. Print it, reverse it, and put the reversed copy in front of the downbeat it was built for.

## Where the monosynth sits in the mix

A monosynth line and a kick drum want the same 60 to 120 Hz, and the loser is decided before you reach for an EQ. Sidechaining the synth to the kick is the usual answer, and it works better on a monosynth than on a pad because one voice ducking is one thing ducking. Our piece on [sidechain compression](https://gazillionindustries.com/sidechain-compression/) is the method.

Level matters before tone. A synth patch can arrive 12 dB hotter than the sample it sits on, and everything downstream then reads as wrong when the real problem is the fader. Set the input level first; [gain staging](https://gazillionindustries.com/gain-staging/) is the unglamorous half of every synth sound.

Then saturation, and only a little. A bass line with a few added harmonics stays audible on a laptop speaker where the fundamental never arrives at all, and [a small amount of drive](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-use-saturation/) does that job more cleanly than boosting 800 Hz. Drive after the filter, not before, unless you want the filter to tame what the drive adds.

## What a monosynth costs you

Every instrument has a bill. This one arrives in four parts and all four are worth knowing before you spend.

It costs chords. One voice means one note, so pads, stabs and anything harmonic needs a second instrument or a second instance. Producers who work mainly in chords tend to find a monosynth frustrating for about a week, and then keep it for the bass.

It costs arrangement space. A monosynth line is loud, narrow and insistent by nature, and two of them in the same register will fight for the whole record. Give each one a filter setting that puts it somewhere the other is not, and check the result in mono, where [phase problems](https://gazillionindustries.com/phase-cancellation/) between two similar parts show up first.

It costs setup time. Programs get you started, but the difference between a good monosynth line and a generic one is almost always five minutes spent on envelope times and glide, and there is no preset for the tempo of your song.

It costs low end discipline. A single voice at 41 Hz with the filter open carries real energy, and your limiter will find it. Watch the meters while you write rather than after, and read our piece on [headroom](https://gazillionindustries.com/headroom-in-mixing/) if the master is getting quieter every time the bass plays.

## Four mistakes worth not making

These come up in the same order every time, and all four are cheaper to avoid than to fix.

**Writing the line before setting the envelope.** The groove of a monosynth part lives in decay time, not in the notes. Set decay and sustain first on a single repeated note, get it feeling right against the drums, and then write the melody into a shape you already like.

**Using detune as a substitute for arrangement.** Piling on detuned oscillators makes a patch wider and less certain about its own pitch, which is the exact failure in the opening paragraph. Take detune to zero, make the part work, then add back the smallest amount that does something.

**Leaving glide on for everything.** Glide is a gesture and gestures need spacing. A bass line where every note slides reads as seasick after eight bars. Put glide on the two notes that deserve it by overlapping only those, and leave the rest stepping.

**Judging the patch inside the loop.** A monosynth sound that is perfect on repeat is usually too bright and too long across three minutes. Print it, play the whole arrangement, and take a third of the filter envelope away. The version that feels slightly under-done in the loop is the one that survives the record.

## Questions people ask

### What is the best monosynth VST?

The one whose envelopes are fast enough for a percussive attack, whose filter stays usable with resonance high, and whose glide you can predict. Those three decide how it behaves on real material; oscillator count and preset totals decide almost nothing. JOURNEYMAN is $59 and carries all three, with three oscillators, two ladder filters with a spacing control, and 200 programs. Test any candidate with the ten steps above before you spend.

### What is the best mono synth VST for bass?

One with low-note priority, constant-rate glide and a filter that keeps its low end when resonance rises. Bass is where note priority stops being trivia: hold a root and play a passing note above it, and low-note priority keeps the root while high-note priority jumps. Set the cutoff around 400 Hz with a second oscillator adding harmonics above, then check the result on a phone before you decide it works.

### What is the best free monosynth plugin?

Surge XT, with Odin 2 close behind. Both are free and open source, both run as VST3 on Windows and Mac with AU on Mac, and both are polyphonic engines you hold to one voice. What you give up is the glide and note-priority behavior that a monosynth is built around, which is a real loss on bass and barely noticeable on a lead.

### Is a mono synth plugin worth it when my synth already has a mono mode?

Sometimes. A mono mode on a polysynth usually gives you one voice and a glide control and stops there. A monosynth plugin gives you note priority, single and multi trigger, and a panel laid out for a single line, which means you reach the control you want without opening a menu. If you only need a one-voice pad, the mono switch is fine.

### How many oscillators does a monosynth actually need?

Two will make almost every sound; three makes them faster. One oscillator plus noise covers percussion and clean sub. Two lets you detune, or stack an octave. The third is for the fifth on a lead, for a sub octave under a detuned pair, or as an FM source aimed at one of the others. Past three you are usually solving an arrangement problem with a synth control.

### Why does my monosynth sound thin next to a polysynth?

Because a chord has three or four notes of energy and a line has one. The fix is not more detune. Add an octave below in the mixer, open the filter another few hundred hertz, and add a small amount of saturation so the harmonics fill the space that the missing notes were filling. Then check it against the drums rather than solo.

### Do I need a MIDI keyboard to use a monosynth plugin?

No, but glide and trigger modes are hard to set by drawing notes, because both depend on how much two notes overlap. You can do it in the piano roll by dragging note ends past the next note start. A keyboard makes it five minutes instead of thirty, and any two-octave controller is enough for a bass line.

### Can a monosynth plugin make drums?

Yes, and it is the fastest way to a kick that belongs to your track rather than to a pack. Triangle oscillator, pitch modulation with a very short decay, volume envelope at zero attack and around 40 ms decay. Layer it under an existing sample so the sample keeps the character and the synth supplies the weight.

# Best synth VST for hip hop

Three in the morning, headphones off, the beat playing out of the laptop speakers while you look for your keys. The drums are still there. The bass line you spent an hour on has gone, and what is left is a thin buzz where a note used to be.

The best synth VST for hip hop is a monosynth: two or three oscillators, a resonant lowpass filter, and an envelope fast enough to stay out of the drums' way. One voice at a time is what the bass lines and the leads in this music are actually made of. Ours is JOURNEYMAN, $59 for Mac and Windows. Free ones exist, and they are named further down.

## The short version

- **What to look for**: two or three oscillators, a resonant lowpass, an envelope that opens fast

- **How many voices**: one is plenty for bass and leads; save polyphony for keys and pads

- **For trap**: glide between notes, and a filter that moves on every note you play

- **Free route**: Vital's Basic tier and Surge XT, both free from their own makers

- **What kills a patch**: writing in an octave no phone, laptop or earbud can reproduce

- **Our answer**: JOURNEYMAN, $59: three oscillators, two ladder filters, 200 programs

## The three jobs a hip hop synth has to do

Sort the job before you shop. Almost every synth sound in rap, trap, drill and boom bap falls into one of three roles, and the instrument that serves one of them well is often mediocre at the others. Knowing which one you are hiring for cuts the field by about two thirds before you download anything.

**Bass.** One note at a time, low, loud, and carrying the harmony on its own. This is the role that decides whether the beat works in a car, and it is the one people most often try to fill with a preset built for a different genre. It needs a clean low fundamental, a filter you can park low, and an envelope that lets go before the next kick.

**Leads and hooks.** Also one note at a time, usually in a narrow window between 1 kHz and 4 kHz where nothing else in the beat lives. Bells, flutes, plucked synths, the melody that gets stuck in someone's head. Here the sound has to be distinctive within about three notes, because that is all a hook gets.

**Keys, pads and texture.** Chords under the top line, held and filtered back so they read as air rather than as parts. This is the only one of the three that genuinely wants polyphony, and it is also the one a sample will often do better than a synth will.

Two of the three roles are monophonic by nature. That is the whole reason the answer to "best synth plugins for hip hop" keeps coming back to a one-voice instrument instead of the biggest library on the market.

## Why the best synth plugins for hip hop are mostly one voice

A monosynth plays one note at a time and puts everything it has behind that note. Every oscillator, the whole filter, the whole envelope, one pitch. When you play a second key before releasing the first, the instrument does not start a new voice; it slides the one voice it has to the new pitch, and that slide is a musical event rather than a limitation.

The practical consequence is level. Three oscillators stacked on one note, detuned a few cents apart, produce a single fat pitch with a slow beat in it. Split those same three oscillators across a three-note chord and you have one thin oscillator per note, three pitches fighting for the same low register, and a low end that turns to mud the moment the kick lands.

The second consequence is glide. Hand a monosynth two overlapping notes and it travels between them. A polysynth starts a second voice and leaves the first to decay. Every sliding bass figure in trap, drill and modern rap depends on that first behavior, which is why producers who have never used a hardware synth still end up wanting a monophonic one.

There is a third consequence and it is unglamorous: fewer voices means less to go wrong. One set of controls, one signal path, one thing to hear. When a patch is wrong you can find the wrong part, because there is only one of everything.

## What the controls do, in the order you touch them

Subtractive synthesis is a short list of stages in a fixed order, and every synth in this article runs some version of it. Oscillators make a raw tone rich in harmonics. A mixer sets how much of each one you get. A filter removes part of that spectrum. Envelopes decide when the filter and the volume move. Everything else is modulation on top.

Top left makes the sound, top right takes things away from it. Under the blue headers is modulation; under the cream ones is how it gets played.

**Oscillators and octave.** Pitch is set twice: once by the key you press and once by the octave switch, marked in feet on JOURNEYMAN's three oscillators. Play C2 at 8' and the fundamental is 65.41 Hz. The same key at 16' is 32.70 Hz, and at 32' it is 16.35 Hz, which is under the bottom of human hearing and under the bottom of every consumer speaker ever sold. The octave switch is where most weak bass patches are lost, before a single filter is touched.

**Wave.** A triangle is nearly pure and gives you a fundamental with very little above it. A saw contains every harmonic. A square contains only the odd ones, which is why it reads as hollow and woody. A narrow pulse is thin and nasal and cuts through a busy mix at low level. JOURNEYMAN puts that whole range on one continuous WAVE knob per oscillator, from triangle through saw and square to pulse, so you can sweep it and stop where the note sounds right instead of picking from a list.

**Detune.** Two oscillators at slightly different pitches beat against each other at the difference frequency. Offset them by 8 cents and two oscillators at 110 Hz drift apart by about 0.51 Hz, one slow swell roughly every two seconds. That single number is most of what people mean by a synth sounding fat. On JOURNEYMAN the FREQUENCY knobs on oscillators two and three do this against oscillator one.

**Filter.** A lowpass filter passes what is below the cutoff and attenuates what is above it, at a slope set by how many poles it has. A pole is 6 dB per octave in the textbook sense, so a three-pole and a four-pole setting land an octave above cutoff 6 dB apart, which is half the amplitude. JOURNEYMAN has two ladder filters, one per channel, with a shared CUTOFF, a SPACING control that offsets one from the other, RESONANCE, and a poles switch for each. The long version of what cutoff and resonance do lives in [filter cutoff and resonance explained](https://gazillionindustries.com/filter-cutoff-and-resonance/).

**Envelopes.** Attack, decay, sustain and release, twice: one set moving the filter, one set moving the volume. In beat production the filter envelope is doing most of the character work. A short decay with the amount turned up gives you the click and thump that lets a bass note read as percussive rather than as a held tone.

[JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html) is our monosynth for Mac and Windows: one voice, three oscillators, two ladder filters, two envelopes, two modulation busses and 200 programs across basses, leads, keys, pads, percussion and fx, for $59. Every program is already wired to the mod wheel and the touch surface, so the patches move before you have learned a single knob. There's a demo on the page.

## Best synth VST for trap: glide, filter and the low octave

Trap asks a synth for two specific things. The first is pitch that travels between notes instead of jumping. The second is a low register that survives being played back on hardware designed for podcasts.

Glide is the easy half. Turn it on, set the rate, play overlapping notes, and the pitch ramps from one to the next. The rate is the whole performance: too fast and it is a blip, too slow and the note arrives late over the bar line. JOURNEYMAN puts GLIDE on a switch with GLIDE RATE beside it, and the trigger mode matters as much as the rate, because single trigger is what lets a legato phrase slide without retriggering the envelope on every key.

The low register is the hard half. A phone speaker is a few millimeters across and produces almost nothing under a few hundred hertz; a laptop is not much better. A note at 32.70 Hz is inaudible on both, but its harmonics at 65.4, 98.1 and 130.8 Hz are not, and those harmonics are what tell a listener the pitch. So you write the part low and then make sure the harmonics exist, either by choosing a wave that already has them or by adding them afterwards.

Adding them afterwards is a saturation job rather than a synthesis job, and it is covered properly in [how to make bass audible on phone speakers](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-bass-audible-on-phone-speakers/) and [how to distort 808s without losing the low end](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-distort-808s/). The same arithmetic applies to a synth bass and to a sampled one.

Pitch and time on the sub itself is a third thing again, and for slides that bend the whole sample rather than the note, see [how to pitch a sample](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-pitch-a-sample/).

## Best free synth VST for hip hop

Two free synths are worth the download, and one of them is probably already on your machine.

**Vital.** A spectral-warping wavetable synth. The Basic tier is free and its own page describes it as the full synth with all features, with 75 curated presets and 25 wavetables; the paid tiers add presets, wavetables and skins rather than capability. For wavetable leads and modern plucks it is genuinely strong and costs nothing.

**Surge XT.** Open source, free, and unusually deep for the price. Its own site describes it as a subtractive hybrid where every patch holds two scenes, each a separate copy of the synthesis engine, and ships over 2,800 factory patches. If you like reading a manual, this is the most instrument per zero dollars on offer.

**Whatever your DAW already ships.** Every major DAW includes at least one subtractive instrument, and it will do the three jobs above at a passable level. Open the instrument list before you open a browser. There is a broader list of what is worth installing in [best free VST plugins](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-free-vst-plugins/).

Here is the honest limit of the free route. Free synths in 2026 are aimed at wavetable sound design, and the free ones are excellent at it. None of them is built as a one-voice instrument with the controls laid out in playing order, and that shape is the thing that makes a bass line come out of your hands rather than out of a preset list. Our free plug-in is a compressor rather than a synth, so on this page we are not going to pretend otherwise: for the synth itself we are asking $59.

## Best synth plugins for hip hop that people actually name

These are the names that come up in every thread. Prices below were read on each maker's own page while this was written; they move, so check before you buy.

**Xfer Serum 2.** $249 on Xfer's own store, with wavetable, multisample, sample, granular and spectral oscillator types in one instrument. It is also four times the price of a monosynth, and a bass note uses one of those five oscillator types.

**Arturia Pigments.** 199$ on Arturia's own page, with six synthesis methods across three engine slots, sixteen filter types and over 1,700 presets. A sound designer's instrument. The color-coded interface is the best in the category for seeing a modulation route at a glance.

**LennarDigital Sylenth1.** €139 excluding VAT on LennarDigital's store, or €9.95 a month until it is paid off. Four unison oscillators, eight unison voices each, so 32 voices on a single note, with two filter sections and seven master effects. It has been the supersaw workhorse for well over a decade and it still is.

**Spectrasonics Omnisphere.** The flagship instrument in that catalog, combining several kinds of synthesis with a very large factory sound collection, currently 18 libraries. Its price would not load on Spectrasonics' own page while this was written, so we are not going to quote one. Treat it as a sound library that happens to synthesize.

Every one of those is a good instrument. None of them is a one-voice synth, and if the job in front of you is a bass line or a hook, you are buying an enormous amount of machinery to play one note at a time. That is the gap JOURNEYMAN is in, at $59, which is roughly a quarter of the price of the first one on that list.

## Build a bass patch: the steps

Do this once from scratch and the rest of the instrument stops being mysterious. Values below are starting points on JOURNEYMAN's 0 to 10 knobs; the same sequence works on any subtractive synth with the controls renamed.

- Press INIT to start from a blank program.

- In the MIXER, switch OSC 1 on and set it to 10. Leave OSC 2, OSC 3, NOISE and EXT IN off.

- Set OSC 1 OCTAVE to 16'.

- Set OSC 1 WAVE to 0 for a triangle, then raise it to about 3 for a saw.

- Switch OSC 2 on in the MIXER at 8 and set its OCTAVE to 16'.

- Turn OSC 2 FREQUENCY until you hear one slow beat about every two seconds.

- Set the filter switch to DUAL LP and set both FILTER A POLES and FILTER B POLES to 4 POLE.

- Set CUTOFF to 2, RESONANCE to 0 and SPACING to center.

- Set VOLUME ENV to ATTACK 0, DECAY 4, SUSTAIN 8, RELEASE 1.

- Set FILTER ENV to ATTACK 0, DECAY 3, SUSTAIN 0, RELEASE 1, and AMOUNT to about 3.

- Set KB AMT to 5 so the filter opens as you play up the keyboard.

- Set KEYBOARD to LAST, TRIGGER to SINGLE, switch GLIDE on and set GLIDE RATE to 2.

- Play the part and watch the OVERLOAD lamp. If it lights, lower the MIXER channels rather than MASTER.

- Bounce eight bars and play them back on a phone before you change anything.

The last step is the one people skip, and it is the only one that tells you the truth. The patch that sounded enormous in headphones at step twelve is the same patch that disappeared at three in the morning by the front door.

## Leads, keys and the rest of the 200 programs

A lead patch is the bass patch with three things moved. Take the octave up to 8' or 4', open the cutoff until the tone is bright enough to hear against the drums, and shorten the volume decay so notes stop rather than smear. Add resonance last, in small amounts, because resonance near the cutoff is the fastest way to make a synth sound cheap.

Keys and pads are the awkward case on a monosynth, and the honest answer is to play them as parts rather than as chords: a root line and a separate top line, recorded twice, panned apart. That is more work than holding a triad, and it also sounds less like a preset. Producers who work this way have been doing it for thirty years, which is part of why the beats in [Dilla type beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-dilla-type-beats/) and [Madlib type beats](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-madlib-type-beats/) have the harmonic looseness they do.

JOURNEYMAN ships 200 programs covering basses, leads, keys, pads, percussion and fx, which is an average of around 33 per category. They are a starting point and a teaching aid: load one, look at where the knobs landed, and work backward. Every one of them is wired to the mod wheel and to the touch surface, so the patch responds to a gesture before you have learned what any control does.

The touch surface is the part people use longest. X moves cutoff, Y moves the spacing between the two filters, and the vertical travel of your finger brings in resonance, all three printed under the pad. It turns a static patch into a performance without automation lanes, and it records as automation if you want it to.

## What a monosynth costs you

One voice means one voice. You cannot hold a chord, you cannot let a note ring under the next one, and you cannot build a pad by stacking fifths in a single instance. Every chord becomes a second track, and every track is another fader, another bounce and another decision. On a busy session that adds up.

You also give up the preset economy. A wavetable synth with 1,700 presets is a browsing instrument; you scroll until something is interesting and then write to it. A monosynth with 200 programs is a playing instrument, and if you work by browsing, the smaller list will feel thin for the first week.

And there is no sample engine here. If the sound you need is a rhodes, a flute or a vinyl string stab, this is the wrong tool and a sampler is the right one. A synth that claims to do everything usually does the thing you need adequately and nothing memorably.

## After the synth: getting it into the beat

A synth part almost never sits right raw. Three moves fix most of it, in this order.

First, level and headroom. Synths run hot and a patch with three oscillators open can be 10 dB louder than the sampled parts around it. Set it before you process it; the reasoning is in [gain staging](https://gazillionindustries.com/gain-staging/).

Second, harmonics. A synth bass that vanishes on small speakers needs content above the fundamental, and saturation is how you get it. BEEFY is our saturation, soft clipping and loudness plug-in, $19, with JUICE, BEEF and COOK on the front and SOFT CLIP and LIMIT as output stages. Working method is in [how to make a synth sound thicker](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-a-synth-sound-thicker/) and [how to make bass fatter](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-bass-fatter/).

Third, the drums around it. If the synth and the kick are arguing, the fix is usually on the drum bus rather than on the synth. DRUGS is our one-knob bus compressor for drums, free for Mac and Windows, with DOSE, a GAIN control and a soft ceiling on the output. It is a single knob and it is the cheapest thing on this page. Background in [glue compression](https://gazillionindustries.com/glue-compression/), and the ducking move in [sidechain compression](https://gazillionindustries.com/sidechain-compression/).

If the low end still will not behave with both a synth bass and a sampled sub in the arrangement, the problem is arrangement rather than processing, and [how to mix kick and 808](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-mix-kick-and-808/) goes through it note by note.

## Questions people ask

### What is the best synth VST for hip hop?

A monosynth with two or three oscillators, a resonant lowpass filter and fast envelopes, because two of the three synth roles in this music are monophonic. Ours is JOURNEYMAN at $59 for Mac and Windows, with three oscillators, two ladder filters, glide and 200 programs. If you want wavetable sound design rather than a played bass line, Serum 2 and Pigments are the deeper instruments and cost a good deal more.

### What are the best synth plugins for hip hop if I only buy one?

Buy for the role you fill most often. If that is bass and hooks, which for most beatmakers it is, one monophonic synth covers more of your week than a large library will. If you make beats that live on held chords and evolving texture, buy the wavetable instrument instead and accept that the bass will take an extra step.

### What is the best free synth VST for hip hop?

Vital's Basic tier, which its own page lists as the full synth with all features, 75 presets and 25 wavetables at no cost. Surge XT is the other one, open source and free, with over 2,800 factory patches. Before either, check the instrument your DAW already installed. Free will get you a long way on leads and textures, and a little less far on a played monophonic bass.

### What is the best synth VST for trap?

The one with glide on the front panel and a trigger mode that does not restart the envelope mid-phrase. Sliding pitch between overlapping notes is the defining gesture of the style, and a polyphonic synth answers those overlapping notes with new voices instead. JOURNEYMAN has GLIDE with its own rate control, selectable note priority and single or multi trigger, which is the combination that makes slides play cleanly.

### What are the best synth plugins for trap bass specifically?

For a synthesized trap bass you want a low octave, a triangle or saw, a lowpass parked low, a short filter decay for the thump and glide for the slides. That is a small feature list and almost any monosynth has it; what differs is how quickly you can get there. After the synth, the bass needs harmonics to survive small speakers, which is a saturation step rather than a synth setting.

### Do you need a polyphonic synth to make beats?

No, and most producers use polyphony less than they expect. Bass is monophonic, hooks are monophonic, and chords are frequently sampled rather than played. When you do want a pad, record the monosynth twice as two lines and pan them apart; you get a wider result than a triad in one instance, at the cost of one extra pass.

### Is Serum worth it for hip hop?

For wavetable leads, screaming risers and modern sound design, yes, and its own page prices Serum 2 at $249 with lifetime free updates. For a bass line, you are buying five oscillator types to use one. Plenty of people own both a large wavetable synth and a small monophonic one, and use the small one more days of the week.

### Where should you download synth plugins?

From the maker's own site, always. These searches land on aggregator pages that reprint the developer's blurb word for word, wrap it in a download button, and sit years behind the current version. Read about a synth wherever you find it, then go to the developer and get the file there.

Two in the morning, the beat is finished except for the bass, and you are forty presets deep into the synth that came with the DAW. Every one of them is close. None of them is the note you heard on the walk home.

Under $100 the field splits cleanly. The free synths are complete instruments you can finish records on, and the best-known paid ones sit well above the line — Serum 2 is $249 on Xfer's own page, Pigments is $199 on Arturia's. What a hundred dollars buys is focus: one idea, finished, with every stage on the panel. If the point is to learn how a synth works rather than to shop presets, start with a monosynth. Ours is JOURNEYMAN, $59.

## The short version

- **What under $100 buys**: focus — fewer engines, every control visible at once

- **Free first**: Vital's Basic tier and Surge XT cost nothing and are whole synths

- **Best to learn on**: one voice, one signal path, no menu diving

- **The tell**: after an hour you can say what every knob did

- **The step up**: $199 to $249 territory, and you do not need it yet

- **Our answer**: JOURNEYMAN, $59, one voice and three oscillators

## What "under 100" actually buys

Do the arithmetic before you shop, because the bracket is doing more work than people think. Serum 2 is $249. Pigments is $199. Diva is 179 € with a demo you can download first. Against $59 that is four and a fifth times, nearly three and a half times, and a number that changes with the exchange rate. Nobody sells you a bad synth at those prices. They sell you a bigger one.

Bigger costs something other than money. Six synthesis engines and seventeen hundred presets are a catalog to work through, and a catalog is the opposite of a panel you know by heart. The under-$100 shelf exists because a small maker cannot fund six engines, so they build one instrument properly and put the controls where your hands are. That constraint is the whole reason the bracket is worth searching.

There is a budget argument too, duller and truer than the sound-quality one. A $59 synth leaves $41 of a hundred for the rest of the chain, and our compressor, [DRUGS](https://gazillionindustries.com/drugs.html), is free, so that part costs nothing at all. The wider free shelf is in [best free VST plugins](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-free-vst-plugins/).

## Why the best cheap synth VST is usually a small one

A synth teaches you at the rate its panel allows. Turn one control, hear one thing change, and the connection sticks. Open a modulation matrix with unlimited connections, assign a source to a destination through two dropdowns, and what sticks is the software's filing system. Both synths make sound. Only one of them is making you better at this.

You can hear which kind you are holding in about a minute. Close the filter by hand on a sustained note. If the tone darkens smoothly and you can say where it stopped, the panel is telling you the truth. If it steps, zips, or changes character in a way you cannot attribute to the knob you touched, something upstream is moving that the panel never showed you. Cutoff and resonance are the two controls worth knowing cold, and they get their own page: [filter cutoff and resonance](https://gazillionindustries.com/filter-cutoff-and-resonance/).

The practice worth avoiding is scrolling. Preset banks sold as inspiration turn sound design into shopping, and four hundred patches later you have learned one thing: none of them were it. Presets are for starting. The panel is for finishing.

## A monosynth, in the order the signal travels

Every subtractive synth is the same four stages in the same order. Oscillators make a raw tone with too much in it. A mixer sets how much of each one you hear. A filter takes material away. An amplifier decides the shape of the note in time. Envelopes and an LFO move those stages while the note is sounding. Learn that chain once and every synth you ever open is a variation on it.

JOURNEYMAN lays the chain out left to right, which is why it works as the example here. **Three oscillators**, each with its own **OCTAVE** and **WAVE**. Octave is the register: an octave is a doubling of frequency, so the A above middle C at 440 Hz becomes 220, then 110, then 55 Hz three clicks down, which is where bass lives. WAVE is a continuous sweep from triangle through saw and square to pulse, so the harmonic content moves as one gesture rather than as four buttons.

Two switches change what the oscillators do to each other. **1-2 SYNC** has oscillator one restart oscillator two, which forces the second wave to repeat at the first one's pitch while keeping its own shape — move the synced oscillator and you get the tearing sweep that a sync lead is made of. **3-1 FM** points oscillator three at oscillator one's frequency. At slow rates that is vibrato. At audio rates it adds sidebands and gets to bells, clangs and metal faster than any other control on the instrument.

The **MIXER** sits after them, with a level for OSC 1, 2 and 3 plus **NOISE** and **EXT IN**. Noise is what you add for breath on a pad or the chiff on a flute-ish lead. External in is the door: send a drum loop through the synth's own filter and envelopes and the instrument becomes a processor. Bright waves played high on the keyboard are where any digital oscillator gets tested, which is the subject of [what aliasing is](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-aliasing-in-audio/).

## Two ladder filters, and what SPACING does

The filter is where a synth patch becomes a sound. JOURNEYMAN has two of them, one left and one right, sharing a **CUTOFF** and offset from each other by **SPACING**. Pull the two apart and the left and right channels stop filtering the same material, which reads to the ear as width. Push SPACING to zero and the pair line up and the patch goes solid in the middle.

**RESONANCE** lifts a narrow band right at the cutoff, and past a certain point that lift is loud enough to be the loudest thing in the patch. **KB AMT** ties the cutoff to the keyboard so a note two octaves up arrives as bright as the one you set the patch on, instead of getting duller the higher you play. The mode switch gives you **DUAL LP**, two low passes working together, or **HP:LP**, a high pass and a low pass, which leaves a band with the air above it and the weight below it taken out. There is a **3 or 4 pole** selector as well; in the textbook each pole is another 6 dB per octave of slope, so the choice is about how much of the material above the cutoff survives.

Width has a bill attached and it arrives in mono. Two filters offset in the two channels sounds enormous on headphones and can flatten out on a phone speaker or a club sum, so check it before you commit: there is a full page on [mono compatibility](https://gazillionindustries.com/mono-compatibility/), and the mechanism behind the collapse is [phase cancellation](https://gazillionindustries.com/phase-cancellation/). If filter moves are the part you want to get good at, the technique piece is [how to make a filter sweep](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-a-filter-sweep/), and the wider category is in [best filter plugins](https://gazillionindustries.com/best-filter-plugins/).

[JOURNEYMAN](https://gazillionindustries.com/journeyman.html) is our monosynth for Mac and Windows: one voice, three oscillators, two ladder filters, two envelopes, two modulation busses and 200 programs. Every control that matters is on the front panel, which is the point of it. There's a demo on the page.

## Envelopes, the LFO and the two modulation busses

Two ADSR envelopes, and they do different jobs. The **VOLUME ENV** shapes the note: attack near 1 ms gives you a pluck with the click still on the front of it, attack around 40 ms turns the same patch into something that swells. The **FILTER ENV** shapes the brightness, and that is the one that makes a bass sound played rather than typed — a fast attack, a short decay and a low sustain is the whole recipe for a note that opens and shuts. What you are sculpting there is the front edge, covered in [what is a transient](https://gazillionindustries.com/what-is-a-transient/).

The **LFO** has **RATE** and **SYNC**, plus sample and hold among its shapes, which is the stepped random source behind every burbling sequence ever bounced. Sync ties the rate to the host so the wobble lands on the grid. Left free it drifts, and drift is usually the more musical of the two.

Then the part most cheap synths leave out. Two **modulation busses**, one on the **MOD WHEEL** and one on a **PEDAL/ON** input, each with four choices: **SOURCE**, **SHAPING**, **DESTINATION** and **AMOUNT**. That is a performance control you set once and then play, rather than automation you draw afterwards. The **TOUCH SURFACE** is the same idea with two dimensions: X moves the cutoff, Y moves the spacing, so one drag opens the filter and widens the pair in a single gesture. **GLIDE**, keyboard **TRIGGER** modes and a **BEND** range finish the playing side.

## Why one voice is the best VST synth to learn on

One voice means every note you play goes down the same path, so cause and effect stay legible. On a sixteen-voice synth, a filter envelope you set too slow gets masked by the note before it still ringing. On a monosynth there is nothing to hide behind. You hear your own settings, which is uncomfortable for about a week and then becomes the reason you improve.

It also changes how you play. Trigger mode decides what happens when you hold one key and press another: retrigger starts the envelopes again, single trigger lets the new note take over the one already sounding. Put GLIDE on top of single trigger and you get the slide that no amount of pitch automation ever quite sounds like, because your fingers are setting the timing.

Here is the cost, stated flat: you cannot play a chord. A monosynth gives you one note at a time, so pads, stacks and held triads are somebody else's job. Two things make that survivable. Basses, leads, hooks and percussion are most of what a producer actually needs from a synth, and where you do want thickness you record the part twice with different settings, which gives you a chord you voiced deliberately. The general method is in [how to make a synth sound thicker](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-a-synth-sound-thicker/).

## What makes a good synth VST for beginners

Five things, and price is not one of them.

**A knob for every stage.** If a control exists, it should be visible without a tab. Hidden pages are fine on an instrument you already know and fatal on one you are learning.

**Presets filed by job.** Basses, leads, keys, pads, percussion, fx. A bank sorted by job is a teaching aid, because you can open two basses and compare the panels. A bank sorted by the sound designer's mood is a shopping catalog.

**A standalone version.** Learning a synth inside a DAW means learning two things at once. JOURNEYMAN runs standalone on macOS alongside AU and VST3; on Windows it is VST3 inside your host.

**Readable values.** A control marked 0 to 100 tells you nothing you can carry. Hz, ms, semitones and octaves are information, and information is what transfers to the next synth you open.

**It runs on the machine you own.** JOURNEYMAN is a universal binary, macOS 10.13 or later, Windows 10 or later, 64-bit. Check that line on any product page before the price line.

## Ten minutes with any synth before you buy it

Do this with the demo, in this order. It works the same on a free synth as on a $249 one.

- Load the synth on an empty track and hold one note for four bars.

- Open the filter cutoff fully, then close it by hand across the full range. Listen for stepping or zipper noise.

- Set resonance to maximum and sweep the cutoff from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

- Set the volume envelope to 1 ms attack and 2 s release, then play one short note.

- Play the top two octaves of the keyboard on the brightest wave and listen for tones that move against the pitch.

- Mute every oscillator but one and name the wave by ear.

- Open ten presets and count how many you can take apart from the front panel alone.

- Bounce eight bars and play the file on your phone.

- Open five instances on five tracks and watch the CPU meter.

Step seven is the one that decides it. A synth you can reverse-engineer from its own presets will teach you for years. A synth whose presets are unreadable from the panel is a sample library with knobs on the front.

## What it costs you

A monosynth costs you polyphony, and that is most of the bill. One note at a time means pads and held chords come from somewhere else, and there is no setting that changes it. Decide whether your next six months of tracks need chords from a synth or bass and leads from one. For a lot of people making beats, the honest answer is the second.

It also costs you the easy option. The 200 programs get you into the right area and the panel does the rest, which is the trade you are making on purpose and the reason the skill transfers to every other synth you touch.

And synth bass eats level. A patch with the filter wide open, resonance up and three oscillators in the mixer will read far hotter than the same part played on a sample, and it will push a master into trouble long before it sounds loud. Set the mixer with your eyes on the meter, not the knob — [gain staging](https://gazillionindustries.com/gain-staging/) and [headroom](https://gazillionindustries.com/headroom-in-mixing/) both apply. Low notes that feel huge in the room can also disappear on a phone, which is its own problem with its own page: [bass on phone speakers](https://gazillionindustries.com/how-to-make-bass-audible-on-phone-speakers/).

## Questions people ask

### What is the best synth VST under 100?

It depends on what you want it to teach you. For a polyphonic wavetable synth at zero cost, Vital's free Basic tier is the one most people land on. For a single instrument you can learn completely and then play, a monosynth is the better shape, and JOURNEYMAN is ours at $59 with one voice, three oscillators, two ladder filters and 200 programs. Both answers are under a hundred dollars. Only one of them puts every control in front of you at once.

### What is the best cheap synth VST?

Cheap and free overlap heavily in synths, more than in any other plug-in category. Surge XT is free and open source and outspecs plenty of paid instruments. u-he Podolski is free and small enough to know by heart. Once you are paying, the question changes from "what do I get" to "what am I going to learn", and the answer is the synth whose panel you can read without the manual.

### What is the best synth VST for beginners?

One with a knob for every stage, presets filed by job, readable values in Hz and ms, and ideally a standalone version so you are learning one piece of software instead of two. JOURNEYMAN meets all four, runs standalone on macOS, and files its 200 programs as basses, leads, keys, pads, percussion and fx so you can open two of the same kind and compare the panels.

### What is the best VST synth to learn on?

A monosynth, almost every time. One voice means you hear your own settings with nothing overlapping them, and the four-stage chain you learn on it — oscillators, mixer, filter, amplifier, with envelopes and an LFO moving them — is the same chain inside every large synth you will open later. Learning it on a big instrument works too. It just takes longer, because the panel keeps offering you somewhere else to be.

### Is a free synth VST good enough?

Yes, and anyone telling you otherwise is selling something. Vital's Basic tier is described on its own page as the full synth with all features, and Surge XT ships over 2,800 patches for nothing. The reason to pay is a specific instrument you want, rather than a general upgrade in quality.

It is worth paying for a shape the free shelf does not cover. That shelf is polyphonic almost end to end. ### Mono or poly for a first synth?

Mono to learn, poly to arrange. Get the chain into your hands on one voice where every change is audible, then add a polyphonic synth when you need chords. Doing it the other way round is why so many producers have used a big synth for two years and still browse presets.

### Do I need a MIDI keyboard to use a synth VST?

No, but a monosynth rewards one more than most plug-ins do, because glide, trigger behavior, bend and the mod wheel are all played rather than drawn. Twenty-five keys with a wheel is enough. Without one you can still program everything from the panel and draw the notes.

## Four things people mean by "best synth VST with presets"

The phrase covers four separate problems, and the answer changes depending on which one you have. Sort yourself before you download anything, because the instrument that solves one of them is often a poor answer to another.

**"I cannot program a synth yet, so give me sounds."** A legitimate position, and the most common one. What you want here is a browser with categories that mean something, patches that sound finished rather than like raw material, and a handful of controls that change the patch in a musical direction without you needing to know what they do underneath.

**"I can program, I want a running start."** Different instrument entirely. You want a patch that gets you eighty percent of the way and then gets out of the way, which means every control visible, no menu diving, and a panel where you can see what the preset did before you undo half of it.

**"I want the sounds I have heard on records."** This is the search that runs as famous synth presets, and it is the one with the sharpest teeth in it. More on that below.

**"I want it free."** Perfectly reasonable, and the free tier of this category is genuinely strong in 2026 in a way it was not ten years ago. There is a section on that below too, with what each free one actually ships with.

## What separates the best synth VST presets from a big folder

Preset count is the number everybody prints and the worst one to buy on. Five things matter more, and not one of them is printed on the box.

**The preset moves when you move.** Play harder, push the wheel, lean on the key, and something should happen. A patch that answers every input with the same sound is a sample with a keyboard attached to it. This is the single biggest audible difference between a bank somebody designed and a bank somebody generated, and you can test it in four notes.

**You can find it again.** Sensible category names, a text search, and favorites. A bank of two thousand sounds with no search is a bank of however many you can remember, which for most people is eleven.

**You can edit it without opening a manual.** Load a patch, see the whole state of the instrument, change one thing. Instruments that hide half their engine behind tabs make preset users out of people who wanted to be synthesists, which is a slow way to lose a skill.

**The bank is small enough to learn.** Here is the arithmetic nobody does. At ten seconds a patch, a 626-preset bank takes one hour and forty-four minutes to hear once. A 1,200-preset bank takes three hours and twenty minutes. A 2,400-preset bank takes six hours and forty minutes, and 2,800 takes seven hours and forty-seven. Two hundred programs takes thirty-three minutes, which is a thing you will actually do, once, and then you will know the instrument.

**The levels are consistent across the bank.** A bank that jumps ten or twelve dB between neighboring patches has you riding a fader every time you audition, and the loud one wins every A/B for reasons that have nothing to do with the sound. Set your monitoring once and keep it there while you browse; the background on why is in [gain staging](https://gazillionindustries.com/gain-staging/).
